title: Empathic Presence: Tuning In and Listening
overview: Chapter 3 opens Part II of Egan's The Skilled Helper with the two foundation skills of the therapeutic dialogue: tuning in and listening. Egan argues that communication skills are a neglected but key ingredient of helping and that they must serve genuine dialogue (turn taking, connecting, mutual influencing, cocreating outcomes). He explains empathic presence and nonverbal behaviour, gives the SOLER guidelines for visibly tuning in, and corrects myths about nonverbal communication. He then describes active and empathic listening: to clients' experiences, thoughts (points of view, intentions, decisions), behaviours, emotions, strengths and nonverbal messages, integrated into a narrative; how to process what is heard thoughtfully; and how to listen to oneself. The chapter links listening to the key ingredients of successful therapy and ends with the shadow side - forms of distorted listening - illustrated throughout by the case of Jennie and Denise.
objectives: Explain why communication skills are a key ingredient of helping and what Egan's audience 'mini-drama' shows.
Describe the four requirements of true dialogue.
Explain empathic presence and the role of nonverbal behaviour as a channel of communication.
Describe each SOLER guideline, its cultural qualifications and the SOLAR adaptation.
Outline Pentland's honest signals and the six myths about nonverbal behaviour.
Distinguish forms of poor listening from empathic listening.
Apply the experiences-thoughts-behaviours-affect framework to clients' stories, including points of view, proposals and decisions.
Explain how clients' nonverbal behaviour modifies verbal messages.
Describe the four guidelines for thoughtful processing and the helper's internal conversation.
Explain how listening relates to the key ingredients of successful therapy.
Identify and evaluate the forms of distorted listening in the shadow side.

sections.heading: The Importance of Communication Skills in Helping
sections.detailed:
Egan opens by pointing to a gap. There is plenty of research showing that the helping relationship matters, but very little on the actual communication and relationship-building skills a helper needs to build and keep that relationship. He links this gap to a wider social attitude: communication is taken for granted. He illustrates it with a "mini-drama" he has repeatedly staged with large audiences. Asked how important it is for children to develop solid communication and relationship skills on a 1-100 scale, audiences give ratings close to (sometimes above) 100. Asked how society makes sure children actually acquire these skills, they hesitate, and the honest answer turns out to be that we largely leave it to chance.

From this Egan concludes that a solid set of communication skills is a key ingredient of successful helping. Importantly, these are not exotic skills peculiar to counselling. They are extensions of the ordinary interpersonal skills everyone needs in daily life (he cites communication writers such as Adler & Proctor, DeVito, West & Turner and Wood). Ideally trainees would arrive with these basics already in place, so that training would only adapt them to helping. In practice this is often not so, and training or retraining in "therapeutic communication" is the norm (Knapp, 2007). The aim is for these skills to become second nature.

Egan credits Carl Rogers, Bob Carkhuff and Allen Ivey as trailblazers who developed and humanised communication skills and built them into the helping process; their influence runs through the book.

He then previews Part II. The skills covered are: attending (empathic presence), listening, understanding what clients think and say about themselves, responding with understanding, helping clients explore their concerns more fully, helping them stay focused, and helping clients challenge themselves to develop new perspectives on problems and unused opportunities. The companion manual, Exercises in Helping Skills (Egan, Owens & Reese, 2014), provides practice.

Finally, clients too would benefit from these skills, but they often lack them. In fact many clients are in difficulty precisely because they do not know how to set up and maintain healthy relationships nourished by good communication. So the helper must sometimes help clients with weak communication skills learn to engage in dialogue.
sections.simple: Research says the helping relationship matters but says little about the skills needed to build it. Communication skills are a key ingredient of helping, yet they are just everyday interpersonal skills adapted to counselling. Most trainees need training in them, and many clients struggle precisely because they lack them.
keyPoints: Research on the helping relationship says little about the communication skills needed to build it.
Egan's audience 'mini-drama': people rate communication skills near 100 in importance but admit society leaves their development to chance.
Helping skills are extensions of everyday interpersonal skills, not special techniques.
Rogers, Carkhuff and Ivey are named as trailblazers in humanising communication skills.
Part II skills: attending, listening, understanding, responding, helping exploration, focusing and self-challenge.
Many clients are in trouble because they lack the communication skills for healthy relationships.

sections.heading: Dialogue-Focused Interactions with Clients
sections.detailed:
Interpersonal communication competence means more than being good at separate skills; it means marshalling those skills in the service of dialogue (Pareé & Lysack; Seikkula & Trimble). Egan (2012) gives four requirements for true dialogue.

1. Turn taking. Dialogue is interactive: one person speaks, then the other. In counselling, monologues by either party add little value. Endless client stories and equally endless helper lectures have no place. Egan's point is that monologues isolate people while dialogue requires engagement. Turn taking makes mutual learning possible: helpers learn about clients and base interventions on what they understand from the give-and-take, while clients come to understand themselves and learn to face their problems and unused opportunities.

2. Connecting. Two people can talk past each other, producing alternating monologues, which have no place in therapy. What each party says should connect with what the other has just said. The helper's responses link to the client's remarks and, ideally, the client links to the helper's. For the working alliance to be productive both must actively listen and respond to what they believe the other is saying. Later chapters show how to help clients who are weak at connecting.

3. Mutual influencing. In real dialogue both parties are open to being influenced. This echoes the social-influence dimension of counselling from Chapter 2. Helpers influence clients, and open-minded helpers are also influenced by and learn from clients; indeed clients cannot stay "in the driver's seat" without influencing their helpers. Each continually challenges the other to new learning. Fowers and Davidov argue that the virtue of "openness to the other", combined with dialogue, prevents multicultural and other diversity from collapsing into chaos.

4. Cocreating outcomes. Good dialogue produces outcomes that benefit both parties, and counselling is about results. The counsellor neither tells clients what to do nor abandons them to their own devices; the counsellor is a catalyst for problem-managing dialogue in which clients find their own answers. In true dialogue neither party knows the outcome in advance; if the helper has already decided what to tell the client, or the client has already decided what to say and do, there may be a conversation but not a dialogue. Only clients can change themselves; helpers influence and facilitate change through dialogue, and cocreation still leaves clients in the driver's seat.

Egan's integrating point: individual skills are necessary, but dialogue and the collaboration it creates are the integrating mechanism. Such dialogue must be shaped by the Chapter 2 values: it is respectful and empathic, helps clients understand and own their problems, and moves them toward problem-managing change. Exploitative dialogue, he says, is a contradiction in terms.
sections.simple: Good helping is a dialogue, not a set of separate techniques. True dialogue has four requirements: taking turns, connecting what you say to what the other said, being open to influence from each other, and creating outcomes together. The client stays in the driver's seat.
keyPoints: Communication competence means using skills in the service of dialogue.
Four requirements (Egan, 2012): turn taking, connecting, mutual influencing, cocreating outcomes.
Monologues isolate; alternating monologues (talking past each other) have no place in therapy.
Fowers and Davidov: 'openness to the other' plus dialogue keeps diversity from descending into chaos.
In true dialogue neither party knows the outcome in advance; only clients can change themselves.
Dialogue is the integrating mechanism; exploitative dialogue is a contradiction in terms.

sections.heading: Visibly Tuning In: Empathic Presence and Nonverbal Behaviour as a Channel of Communication
sections.detailed:
Empathic presence. In dramatic moments of life, simply being with someone matters: sitting with a friend in hospital or with a man who has just lost his wife comforts them even if little is said. People appreciate attention and find being ignored painful; Egan notes the averted face often signals an averted heart. Yet, paradoxically, we are often careless about attending to others. Helping demands a robust, intense presence. Geller and Greenberg (2012) call therapeutic presence a foundational stance supporting deep listening and in-the-moment understanding. Visibly tuning in contributes to this presence: it expresses empathy, tells clients you are with them, and positions you to listen. Attention is shown both physically and psychologically.

Nonverbal behaviour as a channel. Some people limit their effectiveness by failing to read others' nonverbal messages or to use their own to send or modulate messages (Manusov; Manusov & Patterson). Terrence misses signs of boredom during his monologues; Cynthia does not use nonverbal behaviour to give her messages zest. Researchers have recognised nonverbal behaviour in daily life and counselling (e.g., Mehrabian; Knapp & Hall; Riggio & Feldman; the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior). Highlen and Hill (1984) explained its importance: nonverbal behaviours regulate conversations, communicate emotions, modify verbal messages, carry messages about the helping relationship, give insight into self-perceptions, and give clues when clients (or counsellors) are not saying what they think. Multicultural helping raises the stakes; David Givens (Center for Nonverbal Studies) produced an online nonverbal dictionary, and assuming gestures mean the same across cultures is wrong and sometimes dangerous.

Egan lists eight factors, for helpers and clients alike: (1) bodily behaviour - posture, movements, gestures; (2) eye behaviour - eye contact, staring, eye movement; (3) facial expressions - smiles, frowns, raised eyebrows, twisted lips; (4) voice-related behaviour - tone, pitch, volume, intensity, inflection, spacing of words, emphases, pauses, silences, fluency; (5) observable autonomic physiological responses - quickened breathing, blushing, paleness, pupil dilation; (6) physical characteristics - fitness, height, weight, complexion; (7) space - how near or far a person chooses to be; (8) general appearance - grooming and dress. People constantly "speak" through this language, and effective helpers learn both to use it and to read it.

Helpers' nonverbal behaviour. Before interpreting clients, look at yourself. Your nonverbal behaviour can matter as much as or more than your words and influences clients for better or worse; clients read in it the quality of your presence. Attentive presence invites trust and openness; half-hearted presence breeds distrust and reluctance. Clients may misread you: a distance comfortable for you may feel too close to them, or a silence you intend as thinking time may embarrass them. So part of listening is noticing clients' reactions to your nonverbal behaviour.

Effective helpers are mindful of, but not preoccupied with, their nonverbal stream. Reading your own bodily reactions is a first step (e.g., noticing tense muscles and asking yourself what is making you anxious and what discomfort you are signalling). You can use your body to censor impulsive, inappropriate messages - for instance holding back a sour look when angered, to give yourself time to reflect. This is not phony, because respect for the client takes priority over instinct; not dumping annoyance is different from denying it, and awareness is the first step to handling it. Positively, you can "punctuate" speech with nonverbal messages: Denise leans forward, nods and says "uh-huh" to reinforce Jennie's intention to renew contact with friends. But do not become preoccupied with your body; use it instinctively, so that nonverbal ease reflects inner peace and supports the working alliance.

Finally, tuning-in skills can be learned but are phony unless driven by values such as respect and empathy. What is in your heart matters as much as visible presence; resentment or disinterest leaks through. Egan's own example: a doctor said reassuring words about an invasive procedure, but his rushed manner signalled impatience - the real message was nonverbal.
sections.simple: Simply being with someone is powerful, and helpers show empathic presence by visibly tuning in. Nonverbal behaviour (body, eyes, face, voice, physiological reactions, physical features, space and appearance) is a channel of communication in its own right. Helpers must watch their own nonverbal signals, which clients read as a sign of how present the helper really is, and these signals are only genuine if backed by respect and empathy.
keyPoints: Empathic presence comforts; being ignored hurts. Geller and Greenberg: therapeutic presence supports deep listening.
Highlen and Hill (1984): nonverbal behaviour regulates conversation, communicates emotion, modifies verbal messages, signals the relationship, reveals self-perception and leaks unspoken thoughts.
Eight nonverbal factors: bodily, eye, facial, voice-related, autonomic responses, physical characteristics, space, general appearance.
Nonverbal meanings differ across cultures (Givens' nonverbal dictionary); assuming otherwise can be dangerous.
Helpers should read their own bodily reactions, censor impulsive signals and 'punctuate' messages, without becoming preoccupied.
Visible skills are phony unless driven by respect and empathy (Egan's doctor example).

sections.heading: Guidelines for Visibly Tuning In to Clients: SOLER
sections.detailed:
Egan summarises key nonverbal skills of visibly tuning in with the acronym SOLER. Because communication is highly culture-sensitive, he stresses that SOLER is only a framework to be adapted, and he repeatedly qualifies each guideline as typical of North American culture.

S - Face the client Squarely. Adopt a posture of involvement. In North American culture facing someone squarely signals "I'm here with you; I'm available." Turning your body away reduces contact; even in a circle people turn toward the person they address. "Squarely" is not a military term and should not be taken literally. If facing squarely feels threatening to the client, an angled position may help. The point is the quality of presence, not inches and angles; your body sends messages anyway, so make them congruent with your purpose.

O - Adopt an Open posture. Crossed arms and legs can signal reduced involvement or availability; an open posture signals openness to the client and what they say, and in North American culture is seen as nondefensive. Again "open" can be literal or metaphorical: crossed legs do not prove you are uninvolved, but ask yourself how far your posture communicates openness. Let posture mirror an empathic, open-minded heart.

L - Remember it is possible at times to Lean toward the other. Two people deeply engaged in a restaurant conversation often both lean forward. The upper body is "on a hinge" and can move toward or away. A slight forward inclination says "I'm with you, I'm interested"; leaning back (at worst, slouching) can say "I'm not entirely with you" or "I'm bored." But leaning too far or too soon may frighten a client by demanding closeness or intimacy. More broadly, "lean" can mean bodily flexibility and responsiveness, which can mirror mental flexibility.

E - Maintain good Eye contact. In North American culture fairly steady eye contact is natural in deep conversation and differs from staring. It says "I'm with you; I'm interested." Occasionally looking away is fine - necessary, in fact, to avoid staring - but frequent looking away may hint at reluctance to be with the person, or at your own discomfort. In other cultures much eye contact, especially with authority figures, is inappropriate; Egan notes he learned this from Asian students and clients.

R - Try to be relatively Relaxed or natural. This means two things: not fidgeting or making distracting facial expressions (the client may wonder what is making you nervous), and becoming comfortable using your body as a vehicle of contact and expression. Your naturalness puts the client at ease.

SOLAR. A counsellor trained in the Skilled Helper model, teaching at the Royal National College for the Blind, wrote that eye contact has little relevance with visually impaired clients, but voice direction matters greatly; visually impaired people feel insulted when sighted people talk to them while facing elsewhere. She adapted every letter except E and proposed SOLAR, where A stands for "Aim" - aiming head and body toward the client so that they hear you are attending directly to them.

Egan draws two lessons. People are more sensitive to how you orient yourself to them than you might think, and anything that undermines your "being there" can harm the dialogue; a respectful, empathic, genuine, caring mind-set can lose its impact if clients cannot see it in your behaviour. Second, beginners may become self-conscious, but these are guidelines, not absolute rules to be applied rigidly. Box 3.1 (p. 80) turns visibly tuning in into self-check questions (see the myths section).
sections.simple: SOLER is Egan's acronym for visibly tuning in: face the client Squarely, keep an Open posture, Lean toward the client at times, keep good Eye contact, and be Relaxed. These are flexible, culture-sensitive guidelines rather than rigid rules. A counsellor for blind students suggested SOLAR, replacing eye contact with Aiming your head and body at the client.
keyPoints: S: face the client Squarely - a posture of involvement; an angle is fine if squarely feels threatening.
O: Open posture - nondefensive; crossed limbs may signal less availability.
L: Lean toward the client at times - but not too far or too soon; also means bodily and mental flexibility.
E: good Eye contact - not staring; cultural norms differ, e.g., with authority figures in some cultures.
R: Relaxed/natural - no fidgeting; comfortable using the body for contact.
SOLAR: 'Aim' replaces eye contact for visually impaired clients; SOLER is a framework, not rigid rules.

sections.heading: Advances in the Understanding of Nonverbal Behaviour
sections.detailed:
Egan starts with an analogy: ants and bees signal to each other nonverbally in swarms and hives, not only to "talk" but to make life-enhancing collective "decisions." Current research (Buchanan; Pentland) suggests humans do the same. In therapy these signals form part of the social-influence dimension of helping discussed in Chapter 2.

Pentland calls these signals "honest signals." They are honest because they are largely automatic, autonomic and unconscious, which makes them hard to fake. He groups them into four categories: activity, interest, mimicry and consistency. Egan illustrates two. Activity: when clients or helpers become more active they display more nervous energy, and each can pick this up. Interest: you can gauge how much "skin in the game" people have by how attentive they are to each other; such attention lets them anticipate when the other has finished a point and find the right moment to come in. Pentland and colleagues have built technologies to read and measure this signalling.

Implications for helpers: honest signals influence the other person, and the kind of helper you are comes across through them and is read by clients. Genuineness cannot be faked. Nonverbal signals are therefore at the heart of dialogue, not conversational niceties. Because these signals are sent, received and acted on "in the shadows", they add uncertainty to dialogue - but, as Duncan noted in Chapter 1, uncertainty can add vigour to helping.
sections.simple: Like ants and bees, people constantly send nonverbal signals that shape what happens between them. Pentland calls them "honest signals" because they are mostly automatic and hard to fake, and groups them as activity, interest, mimicry and consistency. Clients read who the helper really is through them, so genuineness cannot be faked.
keyPoints: Ants and bees signal nonverbally to make collective decisions; Buchanan and Pentland find humans do the same.
Pentland's 'honest signals' are automatic, autonomic and unconscious, hence hard to fake.
Four categories: activity, interest, mimicry, consistency.
Honest signals are part of the social-influence dimension of helping and reveal what kind of helper you are.
Signals operating 'in the shadows' add uncertainty, which (per Duncan) can add vigour to helping.

sections.heading: Avoiding Myths About Nonverbal Behaviour (and Box 3.1)
sections.detailed:
Richmond and McCroskey (2000) describe the shadow side of nonverbal behaviour as a set of common myths. Egan lists six, each with a rebuttal.

1. Nonverbal communication is nonsense - all communication involves language, so all communication is verbal. This myth is fading; it fails the test of common sense.

2. Nonverbal behaviour accounts for most of the communication in human interaction. Early studies tried to "prove" this, but they were biased: designed to knock down myth 1, they overreached.

3. You can read a person like a book. Some people, including professionals, want to believe this, but you can read nonverbal behaviour, verbal behaviour and context and still be wrong.

4. If a person does not look you in the eye while talking, they are not telling the truth. Egan's retort is to tell that to liars; the same nonverbal behaviour can mean many different things.

5. Although nonverbal behaviour varies between people, most nonverbal behaviours are natural to all people. Cross-cultural studies disprove this, and it is not true even within one culture.

6. Nonverbal behaviour stimulates the same meaning in different situations. Context is often the key, yet some professionals accept this myth and build interpretive systems on it.

The common thread is caution: nonverbal behaviour matters, but it is neither the whole of communication nor a code with fixed meanings.

Box 3.1: Questions on visibly tuning in. Egan closes the visibly-tuning-in material with self-check questions for helpers: What are my attitudes toward this client? How would I rate the quality of my presence? How far does my nonverbal behaviour show willingness to work with the client? What attitudes am I expressing nonverbally, and verbally? How far does the client experience me as effectively present? How far does my nonverbal behaviour reinforce my internal attitudes? In what ways am I distracted, what am I doing about it, and how could I be more present? He adds that the Exercises in Helping Skills manual offers practice, and that every conversation is a chance to practise.
sections.simple: Richmond and McCroskey list six myths about nonverbal behaviour, such as "you can read a person like a book" and "people who avoid eye contact are lying." Each is false because nonverbal behaviour depends on person, culture and context. Box 3.1 gives helpers questions to check the quality of their own presence.
keyPoints: Six myths from Richmond and McCroskey (2000).
Myth 1: all communication is verbal. Myth 2: nonverbal behaviour is most of communication (early studies were biased).
Myth 3: you can read a person like a book. Myth 4: no eye contact means lying.
Myth 5: nonverbal behaviours are natural/universal. Myth 6: the same behaviour means the same in every situation.
Box 3.1: self-check questions on attitudes, quality of presence, distraction and congruence of nonverbal behaviour.

sections.heading: Active Listening: The Foundation of Understanding, and Forms of Poor Listening
sections.detailed:
Visibly tuning in is not an end in itself; helpers tune in mentally and visibly in order to listen to clients' stories, complaints, points of view, intentions, proposals, decisions and everything else. Listening seems too simple to need explicit treatment, yet people fail to listen to one another remarkably often. Full listening means three things: listening actively, listening accurately, and listening for meaning. Egan adds that listening is not merely a skill; it is a rich metaphor for the helping relationship and for all relationships.

Active listening matters in all human services. Patients judge doctors on medical competence and on the ability to relate and communicate. Hippocrates advised doctors to listen to the patient, who will tell them what is wrong. Despite high-tech diagnosis, listening remains central to health care, and Egan believes Hippocrates would give the same advice today.

Forms of poor listening. Effective listening is not a state of mind like being happy; it does not just happen. It is an activity that requires work. Everyone has been both perpetrator and victim of the following forms of inactive or inadequate listening.

Nonlistening: going through the motions without real engagement. Sometimes we get away with it, sometimes not. Jennifer asks colleague Kieran what he would do about the counselling centre's surge in requests; he admits he is not sure, and she accuses him of not having listened for ten minutes. No helper intends to not listen, but even good helpers drift when hearing similar stories repeatedly, forgetting each story is unique to this client.

Partial listening: listening that skims the surface, picking up bits but not necessarily the essential points. Janice half-listens to Dean, desperate about his job search, describing a disastrous meeting with a recruiter, because he seems uninteresting. Her attempt at understanding rings hollow, and Dean, dejected, wonders aloud whether he is going about his search wrongly. Partial listening can be worse than nonlistening because it involves pretence - it is phony.

Tape-recorder listening: clients do not want their words repeated - a recorder could do that perfectly. They want the helper present psychologically, socially and emotionally, not just physically. When someone accused of not listening protests that they can repeat everything said, the accuser is not comforted. Clients are often too polite, cowed or preoccupied to complain, but it is a shame if your hearing works while you are elsewhere. Clients want a live counsellor, not a recorder.

Rehearsing: novice counsellor Sid, hearing Casey describe "wild dreams," tells himself that dreams cannot be interpreted - missing that Casey is genuinely disturbed. He could capture Casey's emotion without settling the dream-meaning debate. Even experienced helpers stop listening once they start working out how to respond. Effective helpers instead listen intently to themes and core messages; they are never at a loss for a response and do not need to rehearse, and their responses move clients forward. When clients stop speaking they often pause to reflect and then respond. They pause not because they have not listened, but because they have listened and want to respond helpfully.
sections.simple: We tune in so that we can listen, and full listening means listening actively, accurately and for meaning. Listening is work, not a mood. Four common forms of poor listening are nonlistening, partial listening, tape-recorder listening and rehearsing your reply instead of attending.
keyPoints: Full listening = listening actively, accurately and for meaning; listening is a metaphor for the helping relationship.
Hippocrates: listen to the patient and the patient will tell you what is wrong.
Effective listening is an activity requiring work, not a state of mind.
Nonlistening (Kieran); partial listening (Janice and Dean) - worse than nonlistening because it is phony.
Tape-recorder listening: repeating words without psychological, social and emotional presence.
Rehearsing (Sid and Casey): planning a reply stops listening; effective helpers pause because they have listened.

sections.heading: Empathic Listening: Listening to Clients' Stories and Their Search for Solutions
sections.detailed:
The opposite of inadequate listening is empathic listening - listening driven by the value of empathy. It centres on the kind of attending, observing and listening, the kind of "being with", needed to understand clients and their worlds. It may be metaphysically impossible to get fully inside another's world and experience it as they do, but it is possible to approximate this.

Carl Rogers (1980) spoke passionately about basic empathic listening - being with and understanding the other - calling it an "unappreciated way of being." He called it unappreciated because few people develop this deep listening ability and even expert helpers neglect it. His description (paraphrased): it means entering the other's private perceptual world and becoming thoroughly at home there; being sensitive moment by moment to the changing felt meanings in the person - fear, rage, tenderness, confusion; temporarily living in the other's life and moving about in it delicately, without judging.

Such listening is selfless, because helpers must set their own concerns aside to be fully with clients. Rogers also stressed that this understanding remains sterile unless it is communicated. Clients can sense how intensely they are attended to, but they still need to be understood. Egan's chain: empathic listening leads to empathic understanding, which leads to empathic responding (the subject of Chapter 4).

Empathic participation admits of degrees. Helpers must enter clients' worlds deeply enough to understand their struggles and their search for opportunities, so that their contribution to problem management is valid and substantial. Two dangers follow: if understanding is incorrect or invalid, the helper may lead the client astray; if it is valid but superficial, the helper may miss the central issues of the client's life.

The case of Jennie. Egan introduces the running case. Jennie, an African American college senior, was raped by a "friend" on a date. She received immediate counselling from the university Student Development Center and support during the investigation, but she could not prove her case. The rape and the investigation left her shaken, unsure of herself, angry and mistrustful of institutions she expected to support her, especially the university and legal system. When Denise - a middle-aged, middle-class African American social worker counselling for an HMO - first saw her a couple of years later, Jennie had somatic complaints (headaches, gastric problems), angry outbursts at work when she felt exploited, and was otherwise passive and chronically depressed, seeing herself as a victim of society and slowly giving up on herself. Denise is an expert empathic listener, engaged with Jennie's story and present experience, and knows she must be with Jennie every step of the way.
sections.simple: Empathic listening is listening driven by empathy - really "being with" the client to understand their world. Rogers described it as entering the other person's private world and moving in it without judging. Empathic listening leads to empathic understanding and then to empathic responding, and understanding must be both accurate and deep enough.
keyPoints: Empathic listening = listening driven by the value of empathy; a form of 'being with'.
Rogers (1980) called it an 'unappreciated way of being' - entering the other's private perceptual world without judgment.
It is selfless; understanding is sterile unless communicated.
Chain: empathic listening -> empathic understanding -> empathic responding.
Invalid understanding leads clients astray; valid but superficial understanding misses central issues.
Running case: Jennie (rape survivor, depressed, somatic complaints) and Denise (social worker).

sections.heading: Focused Listening: Experiences, Thoughts, Behaviours and Affect
sections.detailed:
Helping is in many ways a "talking game," so the kind and quality of talk are crucial. Listening at its best is both focused and unbiased. Egan offers two aids to focus.

First, the problem-management helping model itself. Because it is not tied to any theory or school, it helps counsellors organise what they hear without prejudice. Problem-management and opportunity-development dialogue is at the heart of helping; helpers listen to clients' stories to help them search for solutions, i.e., life-enhancing outcomes.

Second, a particular view of personality. Pervin (1996) defines personality as the complex organisation of cognitions (thoughts), affects (emotions) and behaviours that gives direction and pattern (coherence) to a person's life. Rasmussen (2005), in a personality-guided therapy series, adds the "activating event" to Pervin's triad. Because clients tell their stories in terms of experiences (activating events), thoughts, behaviours and emotions, helpers are in effect listening to their personalities at work. More precisely, they listen to individual thoughts and patterns of thinking, individual behaviours and patterns of behaving, individual emotions and patterns of emotionality - all triggered by internal and external events.

Bricker, Glat and Stover (2007) argue that familiarity with this schema fosters "clinical mindfulness" and keeps therapy moving toward objective, recognisable goals, whereas a helper with no framework for organising what clients say risks "clinical drift."

The four elements:
- Experiences: what happens to clients (e.g., being fired). Jennie spoke of being raped, belittled and ignored.
- Thoughts: how clients think and the thoughts in their heads. Jennie believed the colour of her skin worked against her.
- Behaviour: what clients do or refrain from doing. External behaviour (smoking and drinking heavily) and internal behaviour (daydreaming). Jennie pulled away from family and friends after the investigation.
- Affect: feelings, emotions and moods arising from or linked to experiences and behaviour (e.g., depression after fights with a fiance). Jennie spoke of shame, betrayal and anger.

These elements are interrelated and clients mix them together. Egan's example: a client tells a personnel counsellor he has had "one of the lousiest days" of his life - the counsellor knows something went wrong and he feels bad, but little else. The client then explains: his boss yelled at him in front of colleagues for not landing an order (experience); he lost his temper (emotion) and yelled back (behaviour); he was fired on the spot (experience); he thinks the boss is a jerk who should not supervise (thought/point of view); he now feels awful (emotion) and is checking whether he can get the job back (behaviour); he intends to fight because it is unjust (thought/resolve). Problem situations become much clearer when spelled out as specific experiences, thoughts, behaviours and feelings in specific situations.
sections.simple: Listening works best when it is focused and unbiased. Two aids help: the problem-management model, and a view of personality as experiences, thoughts, behaviours and feelings (Pervin plus Rasmussen's "activating event"). Having such a framework keeps therapy goal-directed and prevents "clinical drift".
keyPoints: Listening at its best is focused and unbiased; helping is a 'talking game'.
Aid 1: the problem-management model, which is not tied to any theory or school.
Aid 2: Pervin's personality triad (cognitions, affects, behaviours) plus Rasmussen's 'activating event'.
Bricker, Glat and Stover: a framework fosters 'clinical mindfulness'; no framework risks 'clinical drift'.
Experiences = what happens; thoughts; behaviour (external and internal); affect = feelings, emotions, moods.
The 'lousiest day' example shows how clients mix the four elements.

sections.heading: Listening to Clients' Experiences
sections.detailed:
Most clients spend a good deal of time - sometimes too much - talking about what happens to them, for example a society full of "No Help Wanted" signs, drugs being everywhere, or headaches that prevent them doing anything. It is of paramount importance to listen to and understand these experiences.

However, because experiences often focus on what other people do or fail to do, experience-focused stories are often incomplete and tinged - or flooded - with victimhood. The implication is that others or the world are to blame (e.g., a partner who leaves the house a mess "explains" poor concentration at work; a colleague's jokes "make" the client feel bad).

Some clients describe internal experiences that feel outside their control: depression that "comes from nowhere," or "I just can't stop thinking of him." The last sounds like an action but is expressed as an experience - something happening to the client, in the client's own view.

One reason some clients fail to manage their problems is that they are too passive or see themselves as victims - of other people, of immediate settings like the family, of larger institutions such as government or the workplace, of cultural prescriptions, or of internal forces. Feeling out of control, they talk at length about these experiences ("Company policy discriminates against women"; "No innovative teacher gets very far around here").

Egan balances this in two ways. Some clients really are treated unfairly. They can be helped to cope, but full management of their problems may require change in the social settings themselves; one counsellor helped a client cope with a brutal husband, but ultimately the courts had to intervene. For other clients, dwelling on experiences is a way of avoiding responsibility ("It's not my fault"). Sykes (1992), in A Nation of Victims, worried that the United States was becoming a nation of whiners unwilling to take responsibility. Egan calls this too broad, but insists counsellors must be able to tell "whiners" from the truly victimised. Self-pity and whining do little to improve things; helpers must both respect clients' negative experiences and help them move beyond them.
sections.simple: Clients talk a lot about what happens to them, and this must be understood. But experience-focused stories are often incomplete and full of victimhood, blaming others or the world. Helpers must tell real victims from "whiners", respect painful experiences, and help clients move beyond them.
keyPoints: Listening to and understanding experiences is of paramount importance.
Experience stories are often incomplete and tinged or flooded with victimhood.
Some internal experiences feel out of control ('I just can't stop thinking of him' is an action framed as an experience).
Passivity and a victim stance are reasons some clients fail to manage problems.
Some clients are truly victimised and social settings must change (the brutal husband and the courts).
Sykes' 'nation of victims': distinguish whiners from victims; respect experiences but help clients move beyond them.

sections.heading: Listening to Clients' Thoughts: Points of View, Intentions, Proposals and Decisions
sections.detailed:
A lot goes on in clients' heads. Common ways clients share their thinking are sharing points of view, stating intentions, declaring decisions, and offering proposals and plans.

Points of view. As clients tell stories, explore possibilities, set goals, make plans and review obstacles, they share points of view. A point of view is a client's personal estimation of something. A full point of view contains four parts: the view itself, the reasons for it, an illustration that brings it to life, and some indication of how open the holder is to modifying it. If the client also expects others to adopt it, they are engaged in selling or persuasion. Often the implied message is "Why don't others think like me?" or "This is my opinion and I don't care what others think." Example: Aurora, 80, says her dying 85-year-old sister in Florida wants her to come and care for her; Aurora thinks this asks too much because she needs help herself. Her sister's point of view is effectively "my needs trump yours," so she keeps pressing.

Points of view reveal beliefs, values, attitudes and convictions. Clients may hold views on everything, but helpers attend to those relevant to the problem situation or undeveloped opportunities. Jennie says the system - church, government, community, sometimes family - cannot be trusted; if you have problems, you become a problem to others. Denise sees how strongly this view drives Jennie's behaviour and understands where it comes from, but knows Jennie will eventually benefit from examining its unintended consequences, since it may be keeping her locked in misery. Points of view have power, which can be self-enhancing or self-limiting.

Intentions, proposals and plans. Clients reveal their thinking when they state intentions, make proposals or argue for courses of action - all problem-management behaviours. Lydia, a single parent among the "working poor," with no insurance and an absent father of her children, tells a social worker she is thinking of quitting her minimum-wage job, going on welfare and picking up cash jobs, because travel eats her wages and time with her children. She is making a case but stops short of a decision. Her case contains what she wants to do (quit and move into the "alternate" economy), the reasons (inadequate work situation, need to make ends meet), and the implications (less hassle, more time with and benefit for her children).

Decisions. Helping clients review decisions already made and make new ones is a key ingredient of successful therapy. Clients often announce decisions ("I've decided to stop drinking. Cold turkey"; trying online dating). Decisions have implications for the decision maker and others: the man quitting drinking has his work cut out, and his wife, used to coping with a drunk, may now have to adjust to a "new person." Sharing a decision fully means stating the decision, the reasons, the implications for self and others, and whether any part is open to review. Jennie, in a languid tone, tells Denise she will not take any job where she has to fight "the race thing" or "the woman thing," accepting the limited opportunities. This is more than a point of view - it says "I've made up my mind," with an implied command to Denise not to argue. Denise hears this but believes some of Jennie's messages need challenging. Because how a decision is delivered says a lot about it, Jennie's listless delivery suggests it may not be final; a dialogue about reasons and implications can add value.
sections.simple: Clients reveal their thinking through points of view, intentions, proposals and decisions. A full point of view includes the view, reasons, an illustration and how open the person is to changing it. A fully shared decision includes the decision, reasons, implications for self and others, and whether it is open to review. Points of view can be self-enhancing or self-limiting.
keyPoints: Thinking is shared via points of view, intentions, decisions, and proposals/plans.
Full point of view: the view, reasons, an illustration, and openness to modification (Aurora and her sister).
Points of view reveal beliefs, values, attitudes and convictions; they can be self-enhancing or self-limiting (Jennie's distrust of 'the system').
Proposals/cases include what, why and implications (Lydia, a single parent among the working poor).
Full decision: decision, reasons, implications for self and others, openness to review.
How a decision is delivered (Jennie's languid tone) says much about how final it is.

sections.heading: Listening to Clients' Behaviours and to Their Feelings, Emotions and Moods
sections.detailed:
Behaviours and patterns of behaviour. Everyone does things that get them into trouble and fails to do things that would get them out of trouble or develop opportunities. Clients are no different: plotting revenge when ignored, lashing out at anyone who mentions a father in jail, not taking prescribed antidepressants, getting drunk when bored, having unprotected sex with many partners. Some clients talk freely about experiences but are reluctant to talk about behaviours, partly because behaviour raises issues of personal responsibility.

Feelings, emotions and moods. Egan describes them as a river running through us - peaceful, meandering, turbulent or raging; often beneficial, sometimes dangerous, seldom neutral. They are an important part of problem situations and undeveloped opportunities (Angus & Greenberg; Plutchik; Rottenberg & Johnson). Though psychology was once accused of not taking emotion seriously, things have changed: in 2001 the APA launched the journal Emotion. Practical self-help books by professionals (McKay & Dinkmeyer; McKay, Davis & Fanning) take a positive-psychology approach to experiencing, regulating and using emotion. There is also a commercial "anger management" industry, with excellent and trashy programmes; Roffman (2004) rejects anger as a thing to be managed and sees it as a resource. Emotional life is more than anger.

Emotional intelligence. There is a literature on emotional intelligence as a distinct ability (Salovey & Mayer; Mayer, Roberts & Barsade; Ciarrochi), different from the broader writings (Goleman; Egan) on social-emotional maturity; the concept has supporters and detractors (Murphy). The focus here is the ability to make emotions life-enhancing. Mayer and Salovey (1997) describe four branches: accurately perceiving emotions in oneself and others; using emotions to facilitate thought; understanding emotional meanings; and managing one's emotions effectively. These abilities help helpers read their own emotions and help clients with theirs.

Why recognising feelings matters - three reasons. (1) They pervade our lives: almost everything has an emotional tone, including clients' stories, views, decisions and proposals. (2) They greatly affect quality of life: depression stops us in our tracks; escaping self-doubt lets a client breathe. (3) They drive behaviour: Lang (1995) calls them "action dispositions"; angry clients may do desperate things, enthusiastic ones can achieve more than they imagined. We can learn to tune into our own and clients' emotions in order to regulate them.

Emotions highlight learning opportunities: self-pity after a break-up constricts the world; shame after yelling at one's mother may be a wake-up call; recurring anxiety can become a self-perpetuating habit, a vicious circle to break; feeling great after finishing a postponed term paper turns emotion into a tool against procrastination. This last example shows that positive emotions, long neglected in favour of negative ones, are now studied. Salovey, Rothman, Detweiler and Steward (2000) suggest positive emotions promote physical and psychological well-being, can free psychological resources, act as learning opportunities and encourage health behaviours. Since social support matters in problem management, it is notable that clients with a positive attitude elicit more support, while potential supporters shun those overwhelmed by negative emotion.

Clients often express feelings without naming them - excitement in the voice about an unrequested raise, listlessness and a downward gaze signalling depression, a dying person's anger. Others hold feelings back. Effective helpers pick up verbal and nonverbal clues. Feelings colour and give meaning to clients' words; meaning lies in the full package. To name emotional subtleties you need experience and vocabulary; Plutchik offers a wide range of emotions organised around eight basic emotions with coloured graphics.
sections.simple: Clients do things that get them into trouble, but often find behaviour harder to discuss than experiences because it raises responsibility. Feelings, emotions and moods run through everything, affect quality of life and drive behaviour. Emotional intelligence (Mayer and Salovey's four branches) helps helpers read emotions, including those expressed without words, and positive emotions are a resource.
keyPoints: Clients often avoid talking about behaviour because it raises personal responsibility.
Emotions are a river: often beneficial, sometimes dangerous, seldom neutral; APA journal Emotion began in 2001.
Roffman sees anger as a resource, not a thing to be managed.
Mayer and Salovey's four branches: perceiving, using, understanding and managing emotions.
Three reasons feelings matter: they pervade life, affect its quality, and drive behaviour (Lang: 'action dispositions').
Positive emotions aid well-being and attract social support (Salovey et al.); Plutchik offers a vocabulary built on eight basic emotions.

sections.heading: Listening for Strengths, Opportunities and Resources
sections.detailed:
If you listen only for problems, you will mostly talk about problems, and you will shortchange clients. Every client has something going for them, and the helper's job is to spot these resources and help clients invest them in managing problems and opportunities. If people use only a fraction of their potential (Maslow, 1968), there is much to tap.

Egan's example: a counsellor works with a successful 65-year-old businessman who, with his wife, raised three well-educated, successful children, but who is struggling with health problems. The counsellor learns that the man was one of a group of poor inner-city boys in a longitudinal study, with a mean IQ of 80 and many social disadvantages (Vaillant, 2000). Listening, the counsellor hears a history of resilience and helps him review how he coped while growing up. Energised, the man says, in effect, that he never gave up then and has no reason to start now.

A strand of the positive psychology movement focuses on strengths, especially those clients possess but fail to use (Aspinwall & Staudinger; Peterson & Seligman). Lopez and Snyder's (2003) book on positive psychological assessment examines strengths such as hope, optimism, self-efficacy, problem-solving, internal locus of control, creativity, wisdom, courage, positive emotions, self-esteem, love, emotional intelligence, forgiveness, humour, gratitude, faith, morality, coping and well-being. Listening for hints of these capabilities is a first step, and these writers are committed to building a science of human strengths.

Egan's summary line: poor counsellors listen only for problems; successful counsellors search out the client's resources.
sections.simple: Listening only for problems shortchanges clients. Every client has strengths and resources, and the helper should spot them and help clients use them. The businessman from Vaillant's study rediscovered his lifelong resilience once his counsellor listened for it.
keyPoints: Listening only for problems leads to talking only about problems.
Maslow: people use only a fraction of their potential.
Vaillant (2000) example: a businessman who grew up poor (mean IQ 80 group) rediscovers his resilience.
Positive psychology focuses on unused strengths (Peterson & Seligman; Lopez & Snyder's list of strengths).
Poor counsellors listen just for problems; successful counsellors search out resources.

sections.heading: Listening to Clients' Nonverbal Messages and Modifiers
sections.detailed:
Carton, Kessler and Pape (1999) showed that the ability to read nonverbal messages helps people establish and maintain relationships. Having understood their own nonverbal "speech," helpers turn to clients' nonverbal behaviour, which sends a steady stream of clues. The skill is to read these messages without distorting or overinterpreting them. When Denise remarks that talking about herself seems hard, Jennie says she does not mind at all - but she speaks hesitantly, looks away and frowns; the real answer is probably nonverbal. Nonverbal behaviour "leaks" what we really mean, and its spontaneity causes leakage even in highly defensive clients; it is not easy for clients to fake nonverbal behaviour (Wahlstein, 1991).

Besides being a channel in itself, nonverbal behaviour - facial expression, bodily motion, voice quality - modifies and punctuates verbal messages, much as punctuation marks and underlining do in writing. Five ways:

1. Confirming or repeating. When Denise's response hits the mark, Jennie says "That's right!" while her eyes light up, she leans forward and her voice becomes animated.
2. Denying or confusing. Challenged, Jennie denies being upset, but her voice falters and her upper lip quivers; the nonverbal carries the real message.
3. Strengthening or emphasising. When Denise suggests Jennie ask her boss what he means by "erratic behaviour," Jennie says in a startled voice she could not do that, slouching and putting her face in her hands.
4. Adding intensity. Jennie says she dislikes being confronted before being understood, then stares fixedly and silently with a frown - showing her feelings are intense.
5. Controlling or regulating. In group counselling Nina looks at Tom as if to speak to him; he looks away; she hesitates and says nothing. Tom's gesture controlled her behaviour.

Cautions. Egan prefers "reading" to "interpreting": we listen to understand clients, not to dissect them. Merely noticing is not enough; trainees can learn to identify useful messages by watching videotaped interactions, including their own (Costanzo, 1992), followed by practice. Because nonverbal behaviours can mean many things, the key to the real meaning is context. Effective helpers listen to the whole context of the interview and are not seduced or overwhelmed by details. Novices sometimes fasten on a half-smile or a frown, overinterpret it, and lose the person.
sections.simple: Clients' nonverbal behaviour often reveals what they really mean, because it "leaks" and is hard to fake. It also modifies speech in five ways: confirming, denying, emphasising, adding intensity and regulating the conversation. Helpers should "read" rather than over-interpret, always using context.
keyPoints: Carton, Kessler and Pape (1999): reading nonverbal messages helps build and maintain relationships.
Nonverbal behaviour 'leaks' real meaning and is hard to fake (Wahlstein, 1991).
Five modifiers: confirming/repeating, denying/confusing, strengthening/emphasising, adding intensity, controlling/regulating.
'Reading', not 'interpreting': understand clients, don't dissect them.
Trainees learn from videotaped interactions (Costanzo, 1992).
Context is the key to meaning; novices overinterpret single cues and lose the person.

sections.heading: Putting It All Together: Listening to the Client's Integrated Narrative
sections.detailed:
When clients talk about their concerns they mix every form of discourse - thoughts, stories, experiences, emotions, actions, evolving decisions, points of view, proposed actions, strengths and resources. This mix is the client's narrative. Lessons from the narrative therapy movement (Angus & Greenberg; Angus & McCloud; Madigan; Payne; White and others) can help clients integrate it into a coherent story.

The Narrative Therapy Centre of Toronto describes narrative therapy as a respectful, collaborative approach focused on the stories of people's lives, based on the idea that problems are produced in social, cultural and political contexts, and that each person builds the meaning of their life from the stories available in those contexts. Stories consist of events linked by a theme, occurring over time according to a plot. Some events are privileged over others as more important or true; as the story takes shape the teller selects only certain information, so the same story keeps being told.

Narrative therapy focuses on clients' understanding of their stories and how their experiences, thoughts, emotions and actions fit the story's context. It can help clients do three things: bring "untold" parts of the past into their life narrative; emotionally enter and reauthor their own stories; and/or construct new meanings in old stories or find new meanings in stories that emerge in therapy. Egan sets aside its philosophical links to constructivism and postmodernism as not relevant here.

Jennie's reauthoring. Early on Denise sees many self-limiting, even self-defeating themes in Jennie's story. Later, with Denise's help, Jennie begins to reauthor it. Speaking more animatedly and with more eye contact than usual, Jennie describes meeting a woman at work with a story like hers; over dinner she realised the woman had narrowed her world to a small patch to avoid being hurt, and saw she was doing her own version of the same. She decides she must change: she wants to revisit her work and social life, run small experiments in broadening her social life starting with her family, discuss the kind of work she wants without self-imposed limits, climb out of "the hole," and help her friend do likewise.

Egan points out that everything is present: a story with experiences, actions and feelings; points of view about her friend; decisions about her life's direction; and proposals for experiments. A new narrative built on different experiences, thoughts, emotions and actions is emerging.

The point: frameworks for listening help you zero in on key messages and the feelings that permeate them, and the narrative construct helps clients integrate all these elements into a coherent picture. But do not go overboard. You are a human listening to a human, not a vacuum cleaner sweeping up every scrap of information. Effective dialogic listening helps both parties find the meaning needed to move forward in managing problems and developing opportunities.
sections.simple: Clients mix experiences, thoughts, feelings, actions, decisions and strengths into one narrative. Narrative therapy helps clients understand, reauthor and find new meanings in their stories, as Jennie does when she decides to climb out of "the hole". Helpers should listen for the integrated story, but not try to vacuum up every detail.
keyPoints: The client's narrative mixes all forms of discourse, including strengths and resources.
Narrative therapy (Toronto centre): problems arise in social, cultural and political contexts; stories are events linked by theme and plot.
Three helps: include 'untold' past, emotionally enter and reauthor stories, construct new meanings.
Jennie reauthors her story after meeting a woman with a similar history.
Frameworks help zero in on key messages; the narrative construct integrates them.
Don't be a 'vacuum cleaner' - listen dialogically for meaning that moves the client forward.

sections.heading: Processing What You Hear: Understanding Through Context and Identifying Key Messages
sections.detailed:
As we listen we process what we hear; the trick is to be a thoughtful processor. There are many less-than-thoughtful ways of processing (covered in the shadow side), so Egan first sets out guidelines for thoughtful processing. This section covers the first two; the next covers the rest.

Understand clients through context. People are more than the sum of their verbal and nonverbal messages. Deep listening means listening to clients as shaped by the contexts in which they "live, move, and have their being" (Cook, 2012). Nonverbal behaviour should be read in the context of the whole session, and clients should be helped to understand their stories, views, messages and emotions through the wider context of their lives. Tiedens and Leach (2004), in The Social Life of Emotions, argue that emotions cannot be understood apart from the relationships and groups in which they occur. Culture, personality, personal style, ethnicity, key life experiences, education, travel, economic status and other forms of diversity form the context of problems and unused opportunities, and key elements of context enter the story whether mentioned or not. Effective helpers listen through context without being overwhelmed by detail. Developmental frameworks help (Arnett; Egan & Cowan; Qualls & Abeles), and the University of Michigan graduate programme Personality and Social Contexts studies how contexts shape lives (DeAngelis, 2005).

Denise's contextual reading of Jennie: an intelligent African American woman from a conservative Catholic background, loyal to a church that was a refuge in the inner city, a gathering place, and the source of a decent education and a chance at college. College was her first venture into a mostly white, secular culture; she chose friends carefully, but found she was academically closer to average. The rape and investigation strained a fragile social network; she withdrew from family, church and friends just when she needed support, stayed "out of community" after graduating, and is now underemployed as a secretary, which does little for her self-worth. Denise listens through this context without assuming it defines Jennie. The helping context matters too: Jennie may have feelings about talking to a woman quite different from her, and misgivings about the helping professions. Denise links Jennie's headaches (experiences), self-imposed isolation (behaviours) and chronic depression (feelings) to her social history - being religious in a secular school, being an upwardly mobile African American woman in a predominantly white male society - and sees the rape and investigation as social, not merely personal, events. She does not focus narrowly on Jennie's inner world as if it could be separated from her social context, but nor does she get lost in context; she uses it to understand and to help.

Identify key messages and feelings. Helpers must avoid information overload. A thoughtful search for meaning means identifying key factors - key to the purpose of helping, not to some theory. Denise listens to Jennie's experiences, thoughts, actions, emotions, points of view, decisions, intentions and proposals. Jennie describes an intention gone awry: she meant to push her case because some men on campus were "getting away with murder," but realised she was not taken seriously because she was an African American woman; first she was angry, then numb. Later she mentions frequent headaches she tries to tough out without pills, heightened sensitivity to injustice even on screen, and that she has stopped crusading. Questions arise in the back of Denise's mind, based on the listening frameworks: How far are we both discovering what is important? How is the dialogue going? What are the main points? Which experiences and actions matter most? What themes are emerging? What is her point of view? What matters most to her? What does she want me to understand? What decisions are implied? What does she propose to do? The Duncan feedback surveys (Chapter 1, Appendix 1) help greatly; they do not mimic these questions but open a give-and-take feedback process that surfaces issues not yet discussed.
sections.simple: Thoughtful processing begins by understanding clients through the wider context of their lives - culture, history, relationships - without letting context define them or swamp the helper. It also means picking out the key messages and feelings that matter for helping, avoiding information overload. Denise does both with Jennie.
keyPoints: Be a thoughtful processor of what you hear.
Understand clients through context (Cook); emotions are social (Tiedens and Leach).
Diversity factors form the context of problems whether mentioned or not; listen through context without being overwhelmed.
Denise reads Jennie's story through her Catholic, inner-city, college and social history, and treats the rape as a social event.
Identify key messages and feelings - key to helping, not to a theory; avoid information overload.
Denise's background questions; Duncan feedback surveys support the process.

sections.heading: Processing What You Hear: Hearing the Slant or Spin and Musing on What's Missing
sections.detailed:
Hear the slant or spin: don't avoid tough-minded listening and processing. This kind of listening helps clients explore issues more deeply and identify blind spots that need to become new perspectives. Skilled helpers listen not only to stories, views, decisions, intentions and proposals but also to any slant or spin clients give them. Clients' views of and feelings about themselves, others and the world are real and must be understood, but their perceptions are sometimes distorted.

Egan's examples: a client who sees herself as ugly really experiences herself that way, and this must be heard; if in fact she is nice-looking, that too must be listened to and understood. A client who believes he communicates above average when he is actually below average must be understood, but reality cannot be ignored. Tough-minded listening includes detecting the gaps, distortions and dissonance within the client's experienced reality.

Denise sees early that some of Jennie's self-understandings are inaccurate. Jennie says she probably got what she deserved because her ambitions were too high and she was getting beyond her place. That is Jennie's spin on her career aspirations. Understanding how she arrives at this interpretation is one thing; assuming it reflects reality is another. Egan's principle: to be client-centred, helpers must first be reality-centred.

Muse on what's missing. Clients often leave out key elements, and listening frameworks help you spot them. They tell stories but omit key experiences, behaviours or feelings; offer views without what lies behind them or their implications; announce decisions without reasons or implications; propose actions without saying why, what the implications are, what resources are needed, or how flexible they are. Note both what is put in and what is left out.

Examples: Jennie mentions, matter-of-factly, a 20-minute chat with an old girlfriend who tracked her down - but says nothing about how she felt then or now, or whether she wants to stay in touch. In another session she says her brother, who runs a small business, offered her a job and she refused - then abruptly switches to rescheduling her appointment. Denise notes the experience (job offer) and Jennie's behaviour (refusal) but the missing reasons and implications for Jennie, her brother and their relationship.

This is not a hunt for "hidden stuff"; everyone omits details. Because Denise knows what full versions of stories, views and messages look like, she notices missing parts and uses clinical judgment - largely common sense - to decide whether to ask. When she asks why Jennie refused, Jennie says her brother is a good guy and she might like the work, but this is no time to get mixed up with family - another sign of how restricted her social life has become, perhaps ruling out family support altogether. Later chapters show how to help clients fill in missing details.
sections.simple: Tough-minded listening means hearing the slant or spin clients put on events: their experience is real and must be understood, but it may not match reality - to be client-centred you must first be reality-centred. Helpers should also notice what is missing from stories, views and decisions, and use judgment about whether to ask.
keyPoints: Tough-minded listening detects gaps, distortions and dissonance in clients' experienced reality.
A client's experience (e.g., seeing herself as ugly) is real, but so are the facts.
Jennie's spin: she 'got what she deserved' for aiming too high.
'To be client-centered, helpers must first be reality-centered.'
Muse on what's missing: omitted feelings, reasons, implications, resources, flexibility (Jennie's old friend, her brother's job offer).
Not a search for 'hidden stuff'; clinical judgment (largely common sense) decides whether to ask.

sections.heading: Listening to Oneself: The Helper's Internal Conversation
sections.detailed:
The conversation helpers have with themselves during sessions is the "internal conversation." Effective helpers listen to themselves as well as to the client. Without becoming self-preoccupied, listening on a "second channel" helps you identify what you might do to help further and what may be blocking you from being with and listening to the client. Egan calls it a positive form of self-consciousness.

Egan's personal example: a friend who had been in and out of mental hospitals arrived unannounced at his apartment after six months, highly excited, pouring out a torrent of ideas, some outlandish and some brilliant. Egan wanted to be with him but felt very uncomfortable. He began by naturally tuning in, but kept finding himself at the far end of the couch with arms and legs crossed - defending himself against the torrent. He would uncross them, only to find them crossed again minutes later. In retrospect he was concerned for his own security. He has since learned to use the second channel better; listening to his nonverbal behaviour and internal dialogue helps him interact with clients better.

Helpers can use the second channel to listen to what they are "saying" to themselves, to their nonverbal behaviour, and to their feelings and emotions. Messages may concern the helper, the client or the relationship. Examples: noticing that the client is getting under your skin and you need to reset the dialogue; realising your mind is wandering to tomorrow's tasks; recognising that your instinct is to sympathise with a client whose self-pity blocks action, and that you need to raise it, slowly; sensing that a client may not want to change and it is time to test the waters.

This internal conversation is constant; it can be a distraction or a tool. Fauth and Williams (2005) found helpers' internal conversations were generally helpful rather than hindering, from both trainee and student-client perspectives. Clients have internal conversations too. Hill, Thompson, Cogar and Denman (1993) found that client and therapist are more or less aware of each other's "covert processes," but that helpers, while knowing clients left things unsaid, were not good at determining what those things were. Verbal or nonverbal hints sometimes reveal the client's internal dialogue. Helping clients move key points from their internal conversation into the helping dialogue is a key task, discussed in Chapters 4, 5 and 6.
sections.simple: Helpers have an "internal conversation" with themselves during sessions. Listening to it on a "second channel" - thoughts, body and feelings - shows what might help and what is getting in the way, without becoming self-absorbed. Research finds this inner talk mostly helpful, and clients have their own internal conversations too.
keyPoints: Internal conversation = the helper's conversation with self during sessions; listened to on a 'second channel'.
A positive form of self-consciousness, not self-preoccupation.
Egan's example: crossing arms and legs with an excited friend revealed his concern for his own security.
Messages can concern the helper, the client or the relationship.
Fauth and Williams (2005): internal conversations generally helpful rather than hindering.
Hill et al. (1993): each is aware of the other's 'covert processes', but helpers are poor at knowing what clients leave unsaid.

sections.heading: Listening to the Key Ingredients of Successful Therapy: Client, Self, Relationship, Dialogue and Feedback
sections.detailed:
Egan ends by linking listening to the key ingredients of successful therapy from Chapter 1. He illustrates with two cases: Denise and Jennie, and Laura and Karl (a veteran with PTSD who has a "buddy," Peter, introduced in earlier chapters).

Listening to the client. Helpers give full attention to what clients see as important: their stories, expectations, resources, degree of collaboration, struggles with obstacles, ability to voice concerns, reactions to the helper, willingness or hesitation to be in the driver's seat, desired outcomes, understanding of and willingness to engage with the treatment method, emotions, uncertainties and hesitations, and contextual factors affecting their problems, opportunities and participation. Denise listens for signs of hope, especially Jennie's "tiny steps" back into community. Laura notices how strongly Karl praises his phone and Internet contact with Peter, even hinting he gains more from it than from sessions; she treats this as material for their feedback sessions.

Listening to ourselves as therapists. Helpers listen to how they affect clients, their own uncertainties and hesitations, how the client affects them, difficulties, mistakes, their emotions, their genuineness and the effectiveness of their method - without becoming self-preoccupied. Laura accepts that Karl's relationship with Peter may be producing more results than his relationship with her, because client outcomes are the bottom line however achieved; the relationship is not an end in itself. Denise, hearing all Jennie's resources, feels she should encourage Jennie to move more assertively into the driver's seat, as Jennie shows signs of wanting to.

Listening to the relationship. Effective helpers listen to the relationship-in-progress: what is working and what needs attention, the kind and quality of collaboration, the quality of dialogue, mutual influence, "bumps in the road" and how ruptures are handled. Laura sees cues that Karl treats her as an authority figure to be managed rather than a helper-collaborator-catalyst; asked how they are doing, he always says "just fine" and keeps her at arm's length. Because he is clearly progressing, she does not push. Egan's maxim: good outcomes trump ideal relationships.

Listening to the flow of communication and dialogue. Helpers listen to how well they and clients collaborate through dialogue, tailoring their communication by noticing how clients respond, and assessing clients' communication abilities so they can unobtrusively help clients engage fully. Denise sees Jennie's communication skills as a resource for re-entering community. Karl is clumsier and treats conversations with Laura as a power game, but Laura has no need to be "one up," and there is little one-upmanship between Karl and Peter, so she leaves well enough alone for now.

Listening to the two-way feedback between client and helper. Helpers listen to formal and informal feedback on progress toward outcomes and on the quality of sessions, and muse on it. Denise uses formal feedback from Duncan's surveys to explore problem issues. Laura listens to all Karl's "messages," hears his defensiveness and wonders what she might be doing to cause it; by debriefing his sessions with Peter she learns that his progress seems substantial.
sections.simple: Listening also means attending to the ingredients that make therapy work: the client, the helper's own reactions, the relationship, the flow of dialogue and two-way feedback. Outcomes are the bottom line - Laura accepts that Karl may gain more from his buddy Peter than from her, because good outcomes trump ideal relationships.
keyPoints: Listening links to the key ingredients of successful therapy from Chapter 1.
Listening to the client: importance, stories, resources, collaboration, driver's seat, outcomes, emotions, context (Jennie's 'tiny steps').
Listening to ourselves: impact, mistakes, emotions, genuineness - without self-preoccupation; client outcomes are the bottom line.
Listening to the relationship: collaboration, influence, ruptures; 'good outcomes trump ideal relationships' (Laura and Karl).
Listening to the flow of dialogue: tailor communication to clients' abilities (Karl's power game).
Listening to two-way feedback: formal (Duncan's surveys) and informal feedback on progress and session quality.

sections.heading: Listening to the Key Ingredients of Successful Therapy: Method, Decisions, and Assumptions, Beliefs and Values
sections.detailed:
Listening to the flow of the method of treatment. Helpers look for signs that clients understand and can collaborate on the treatment method, and listen for difficulties with any part of it. For both Jennie and Karl the method is the problem-management process of Part III, so their helpers listen to how they grasp and use it - telling stories and exploring concerns, identifying desired outcomes, and exploring ways to achieve them. Helpers also look for clues to clients' commitment to the work. Neither client has trouble with the framework, though Jennie understands its language better and uses it more proactively.

Listening to the decisions being made. Helpers listen to clients' overall decision-making style - for example whether they are "fast" or "slow" decision makers in Kahneman's sense, and fast or slow about the right issues - and for signs that clients grasp the intended and unintended consequences of their decisions. Jennie is thoughtful but does not always review consequences. Karl is abrupt; his decisions can seem to come from nowhere, as when he immediately rejected feedback surveys (though not the feedback process itself). Laura thinks his fast style may get him into trouble and wonders how to raise it. Helpers also stay in touch with their own decision-making style, since responding to clients involves a series of decisions: Denise wonders whether she influences Jennie (and others) too much; Laura wonders whether she should be more forceful.

Research on "naturalistic" or "adaptive" decision making (Klein; Schraagen, Militello, Ormerod & Lipshitz) shows that the fast, on-the-spot decisions of experts such as firefighters and airline pilots make sense under two conditions: they must be skilled and experienced. In helping, counsellors need to be skilled, experienced and principled. Still, uncertainty always haunts decision making, and helpers must be ready for the "complexity and ambiguity" Klein sees at the heart of important decisions. Despite his defensiveness, Karl knows Laura is skilled, experienced and principled.

Listening to the key assumptions, beliefs, values, norms, ethical issues and moral issues in play. This package, which includes culture, often runs through clients' stories directly or indirectly, or is a key issue in itself. Jennie's religious sensitivities are an important subtext; rediscovering what she truly believes and values is a resource for recovery. Karl, from a fundamentalist background, struggles with a religious culture he has set aside but which influenced him during his tours in Iraq and Afghanistan and still affects his recovery. He carries many "musts" from his upbringing, some helpful, some obstructive. His loyalty to church became loyalty to company, platoon and squad, with mixed feelings. Having survived when his buddies died leaves him with a sense of betrayal, even though he does not think he betrayed anyone.
