Helpers must listen carefully to these assumptions, beliefs, values, norms, ethical challenges and moral issues, focusing on what clients see as key and which themes emerge as influential.
sections.simple: Helpers also listen to how clients handle the treatment method, how they make decisions (fast or slow, aware of consequences or not), and the assumptions, beliefs, values and moral issues in their stories. Helpers must watch their own decision style too; fast expert decisions only work when the decider is skilled and experienced.
keyPoints: Method: do clients understand and collaborate on the problem-management process? How committed are they?
Decisions: 'fast' or 'slow' decision makers (Kahneman); awareness of consequences (Jennie thoughtful, Karl abrupt).
Helpers watch their own decision style (Denise: too much influence? Laura: more forceful?).
Klein's naturalistic decision making: fast expert decisions work if skilled and experienced; helpers must also be principled; uncertainty remains.
Assumptions, beliefs, values, norms, ethical and moral issues (including culture): Jennie's religious subtext; Karl's 'musts' and sense of betrayal.

sections.heading: The Shadow Side of Listening: Forms of Distorted Listening - Filtered Listening
sections.detailed:
Listening as described is not as easy as it sounds; obstacles and distractions abound. Some relate to listening in general, others to reading clients' nonverbal behaviour. The forms of distorted listening Egan describes pervade human communication and sometimes creep into the helping dialogue, occasionally several at once. They belong to the shadow side because helpers never intend to listen this way; they slip into it without realising. Yet these distortions block the open-minded listening and processing that real dialogue requires. The book lists six: filtered listening, evaluative listening, stereotype-based listening, fact-centred rather than person-centred listening, sympathetic listening, and interrupting.

Filtered listening. It is impossible to listen to others in a completely unbiased way. Through socialisation we develop filters through which we listen to ourselves, others and the world. Hall (1977) noted that culture provides a highly selective screen between people and the outside world, determining what we notice and what we ignore, and so giving the world structure. We need filters to structure our interactions, but personal, familial, sociological and cultural filters introduce bias into listening, without our awareness.

The stronger the cultural filters, the greater the likelihood of bias. A white, middle-class helper probably listens through white, middle-class filters. This may matter little with a similar client, but with a wealthy, high-status Asian client, an African American mother from an urban ghetto, or a poor white subsistence farmer, the helper's filters may distort. Prejudices, conscious or not, distort understanding. Like everyone, helpers are tempted to pigeonhole clients by gender, race, sexual orientation, nationality, social status, religion, political preference, lifestyle and so on. Self-knowledge is therefore essential, including rooting out the biases and prejudices that distort listening.
sections.simple: Distorted listening is the "shadow side": helpers slip into it without meaning to, and it blocks real dialogue. The first form, filtered listening, happens because everyone listens through personal and cultural filters learned through socialisation. These filters bias what we hear, especially across cultures, so helpers need self-knowledge to spot their own prejudices.
keyPoints: Distorted listening is 'shadow side' because it is unintended and often unnoticed.
Book's six forms: filtered, evaluative, stereotype-based, fact-centred (rather than person-centred), sympathetic, interrupting.
Filtered listening: complete unbiased listening is impossible; filters come from socialisation.
Hall (1977): culture is a selective screen deciding what we attend to and ignore.
Stronger cultural filters mean more bias, especially with clients from different backgrounds.
Antidote: self-knowledge that ferrets out biases and prejudices.

sections.heading: Evaluative Listening and Stereotype-Based Listening
sections.detailed:
Evaluative listening. Most people, even when attentive, listen evaluatively - judging what they hear as good or bad, right or wrong, acceptable or unacceptable, likable or unlikable, relevant or irrelevant. Helpers share this universal tendency. Jennie tells Denise about telling a friend that the rape and investigation are still alive in her mind, though less vivid; the friend replies that this is exactly the problem and she should forget it and get on with life.

Evaluative listening slides into advice giving. The advice may even be sound, but the friend listened and responded evaluatively. Egan's rule: clients should first be understood and only then, if necessary, challenged or helped to challenge themselves. Evaluative listening turned into advice will put clients off. However, there are productive forms of evaluation: judging, once a client's view is understood, that it needs expanding or transcending, or that an understood behaviour pattern needs changing, can be very useful. It is practically impossible to suspend judgment completely, but it is possible to set it aside for the time being in order to understand clients, their worlds, stories, views and decisions "from the inside."

Stereotype-based listening. Egan recalls being referred to by a doctor as "the hernia in 304." People dislike being stereotyped, even when the stereotype has some validity. Labels learned in training - paranoid, neurotic, sexual disorder, borderline - can work against empathic understanding. Personality-theory books supply stereotypes ("He's a perfectionist"), and we even pigeonhole ourselves ("I'm a Type A personality"), often as an excuse.

In psychotherapy, diagnostic categories can take precedence over the clients being diagnosed. Helpers forget that labels are interpretations, not understandings, of clients; you can be "correct" in your diagnosis and still lose the person. What you learn in psychology may help organise what you hear but may also distort listening. Borrowing Gestalt terms, Egan advises keeping the client as "figure" - in the forefront of attention - and models and theories as "ground" - background knowledge used only to understand and help this unique client.
sections.simple: Evaluative listening means judging everything we hear as good or bad, and it quickly turns into advice; clients should be understood first, with judgment set aside for the time being. Stereotype-based listening lets labels and diagnoses replace the person. Keep the client as "figure" and theories as "ground".
keyPoints: Evaluative listening: judging as good/bad, right/wrong, etc.; a universal tendency.
Jennie's friend: 'forget about it' - evaluative listening turns into advice giving.
Understand first, then challenge if needed; productive evaluation exists; set judgment aside 'for the time being'.
Stereotype-based listening: 'the hernia in 304'; training labels can block empathy.
Diagnoses are interpretations, not understandings - you can be 'correct' and still lose the person.
Gestalt: client as 'figure', models and theories as 'ground'.

sections.heading: Fact-Centred Rather Than Person-Centred Listening, Sympathetic Listening and Interrupting
sections.detailed:
Fact-centred rather than person-centred listening. Some helpers ask many informational questions, as though clients would be cured if enough facts were known. It is entirely possible to collect facts and miss the person. The antidote is to listen contextually and focus on themes and key messages. Denise detects in Jennie a "pessimistic explanatory style" theme (Peterson, Seligman & Vaillant, 1988): such clients comment negatively on unfortunate events, saying things like "It will never go away," "It affects everything I do," and "It is my fault." Research indicates people with this style tend to have poorer health, so Denise hypothesises a link between this style and Jennie's somatic complaints (headaches, gastric problems) - a theme worth exploring.

Sympathetic listening. Because most clients are in some kind of misery and some have been victimised by others or society, helpers tend to feel sympathy, sometimes strongly enough to distort the stories they hear. Liz, who had recently lost her husband to cancer, counselled Ben, who had lost his wife and daughter to a tornado. In their first meeting she wanted to hold him. On a long walk later she realised her sympathy had distorted her hearing: she heard the depth of his loss but, reminded of her own, only half heard his implication that the loss excused him from getting on with life.

Sympathy has a clear place in human relationships, but its "use" in helping is limited. To sympathise is in a sense to become the client's accomplice: sympathising as a client describes how awful her husband is means taking sides without knowing the whole story. Expressing sympathy can reinforce self-pity, which tends to drive out problem-managing action.

Interrupting. Egan is reluctant to add interrupting to the list, as some writers do. When helpers interrupt they stop listening by definition, and interrupters often say things they have been rehearsing, meaning they were only partially listening. But because the helping conversation should be a dialogue, he distinguishes benign from malignant interrupting. Cutting a client off mid-thought because the helper has something important to say is malignant. Gently "interrupting" a monologue with a gesture and a remark such as checking that you have understood the several points made is different. If interrupting promotes dialogue that serves problem management, it is useful - though cultural differences in storytelling must be factored in.

Why helpers fall into shadow-side listening, and why it matters. One possible reason is the unexamined assumption that listening with an open mind equals approving what the client says. It does not; open-minded listening helps you learn and understand. Whatever the cause, the outcome can be devastating because a small error at the start can become a huge error later. Egan's image: a building's foundation slightly out of true is invisible to the naked eye, but by the ninth floor the building looks like the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Tuning in and listening actively and open-mindedly are foundation skills; ignore them and dialogue is impossible.
sections.simple: Fact-centred listening collects information but misses the person; the cure is listening for themes, like Denise spotting Jennie's pessimistic explanatory style. Sympathetic listening distorts the story and can make the helper the client's accomplice, reinforcing self-pity. Interrupting can be malignant or benign, and open-minded listening does not mean approving.
keyPoints: Fact-centred listening: many informational questions; you can collect facts and miss the person.
Antidote: listen contextually for themes, e.g., 'pessimistic explanatory style' (Peterson, Seligman & Vaillant, 1988), linked to poorer health.
Sympathetic listening distorts (Liz and Ben); sympathy makes the helper an accomplice and reinforces self-pity.
Interrupting: Egan is reluctant to list it; malignant (cutting off) vs benign (gently checking understanding in a monologue).
Open-minded listening is not the same as approving.
Leaning Tower of Pisa image: small early listening errors become huge later; listening is a foundation skill.

terms.definition: Everyday interpersonal skills extended and adapted to the helping process; Egan treats them as a key ingredient of successful helping.
Communication skills as used in helping; training or retraining in them is the norm for helpers (Knapp, 2007).
An interactive exchange marked by turn taking, connecting, mutual influencing and cocreating outcomes; the integrating mechanism of communication competence.
The first requirement of dialogue: each party speaks in turn, avoiding monologues and opening the way to mutual learning.
The requirement that what each party says links to what the other has just said, instead of alternating monologues.
Openness of both helper and client to being influenced by the other in true dialogue; echoes the social-influence dimension of helping.
Dialogue in which helper and client together reach outcomes neither fully knew in advance, while the client stays in the driver's seat.
Being with another person in a way that communicates attention and empathy; comforting even when little is said.
Geller and Greenberg's foundational therapeutic stance that supports deep listening and in-the-moment understanding of the client.
Attending to clients physically and psychologically so they can see you are with them; it expresses empathy and positions you to listen.
Communication through body, eyes, face, voice, autonomic responses, physical characteristics, use of space and appearance.
Using nonverbal cues such as leaning forward and nodding to reinforce something a client says, e.g., an intention to act.
Acronym for visibly tuning in: face the client Squarely, Open posture, Lean toward the client, good Eye contact, Relaxed/natural.
Adaptation for visually impaired clients proposed by a counsellor at the Royal National College for the Blind, with A for 'Aim' your head and body toward the client.
Pentland's term for largely automatic, autonomic, unconscious nonverbal signals (activity, interest, mimicry, consistency) that are hard to fake.
Six commonly held false beliefs listed by Richmond and McCroskey, e.g., that you can read a person like a book.
Listening actively, listening accurately and listening for meaning.
Listening as deliberate work and engagement rather than a passive state; the foundation of understanding.
Going through the motions of listening without really being engaged.
Listening that skims the surface, catching bits but not the essential points; phony because it pretends to understand.
Being able to repeat a client's words while not being present psychologically, socially and emotionally.
Mentally preparing one's response while the client talks, which stops listening.
Listening driven by the value of empathy; the attending, observing and 'being with' needed to understand clients and their worlds.
Listening organised by a framework - the problem-management model and the experiences-thoughts-behaviours-affect view of personality.
The complex organisation of cognitions, affects and behaviours that gives direction and pattern to a person's life.
Rasmussen's addition to Pervin's triad: the internal or external experience or event that stimulates thoughts, feelings and behaviour.
Bricker, Glat and Stover's term for the organised awareness that a listening framework gives counsellors, keeping therapy goal-directed.
The risk faced by a helper with no framework for organising what clients say: therapy drifts away from recognisable goals.
What happens to clients - what others do or fail to do, or internal events felt as beyond control.
The way clients think and the thoughts going through their heads, shared as points of view, intentions, decisions and proposals.
What clients do or refrain from doing; external (e.g., drinking) or internal (e.g., daydreaming).
The feelings, emotions and moods arising from or associated with clients' experiences and behaviour.
The tendency of experience-focused stories to blame others or the world, often making them incomplete.
A client's personal estimation of something; revealing beliefs, values, attitudes and convictions.
A point of view plus the reasons for it, an illustration, and an indication of how open the holder is to modifying it.
Client statements making a case for a course of action, including what, why and implications, short of a decision.
A decision stated with its reasons, its implications for self and others, and whether any part is open to review.
Ability with four branches: perceiving emotions accurately, using emotions to aid thought, understanding emotional meanings, managing emotions.
Lang's description of feelings, emotions and moods as drivers of behaviour.
Capabilities clients have but may not use (e.g., hope, optimism, self-efficacy, courage); successful counsellors search them out.
The way spontaneous nonverbal behaviour reveals what people really mean, even in defensive clients.
Ways nonverbal behaviour punctuates speech: confirming/repeating, denying/confusing, strengthening/emphasising, adding intensity, controlling/regulating.
Egan prefers 'reading' nonverbal behaviour: we listen to understand clients, not to dissect them.
The client's mix of thoughts, stories, experiences, emotions, actions, decisions, views, proposals, strengths and resources.
A respectful, collaborative approach focusing on people's life stories, holding that problems are manufactured in social, cultural and political contexts.
Clients emotionally entering and rewriting their own stories so new, life-enhancing themes emerge.
Making sense of what is heard through context, key messages, the client's slant and what is missing.
Listening that detects gaps, distortions and dissonance in the client's experienced reality.
The interpretation a client puts on a story or on themselves, which may not match reality.
Egan's principle that to be client-centred, helpers must first be reality-centred.
The conversation helpers have with themselves during sessions.
Listening to one's own thoughts, nonverbal behaviour and emotions during a session; a positive form of self-consciousness.
The unspoken internal processes of client and therapist; each is somewhat aware the other has them (Hill et al., 1993).
Research (Klein and others) showing that fast expert decisions make sense when the decider is skilled and experienced.
Unintended forms of listening that block open-minded listening and dialogue.
Listening through personal, familial, sociological and cultural filters that introduce bias without awareness.
Judging what one hears as good/bad, right/wrong etc. while listening; tends to turn into advice giving.
Listening through labels and categories so that the label takes precedence over the person.
Gestalt terms: keep the client as 'figure' in the forefront and models/theories as 'ground' in the background.
Gathering many facts through informational questions while missing the person; opposite of person-centred listening.
Tendency to describe unfortunate events as permanent, pervasive and one's own fault; linked to poorer health.
Sympathy strong enough to distort what the helper hears, making the helper the client's accomplice.
Malignant: cutting the client off mid-thought; benign: gently breaking into a monologue to check understanding and promote dialogue.

studies.title: Egan's audience 'mini-drama'
studies.finding: Audiences rate children's communication skills near or above 100 out of 100 in importance, yet admit society largely leaves their development to chance.

studies.title: Highlen & Hill (1984): functions of nonverbal behaviour
studies.finding: Nonverbal behaviours regulate conversations, communicate emotions, modify verbal messages, signal the relationship, reveal self-perceptions and give clues when people are not saying what they think.

studies.title: Pentland: honest signals
studies.finding: People send largely unconscious, hard-to-fake signals (activity, interest, mimicry, consistency) that influence others; technologies can now measure them.

studies.title: Richmond & McCroskey (2000): early nonverbal studies
studies.finding: Early studies claiming nonverbal behaviour is most of communication were biased, overreaching in their effort to refute the 'all communication is verbal' myth.

studies.title: Bricker, Glat & Stover (2007)
studies.finding: Familiarity with an experiences-thoughts-behaviours-emotions schema fosters clinical mindfulness; lacking a framework risks clinical drift.

studies.title: Salovey, Rothman, Detweiler & Steward (2000): positive emotions
studies.finding: Positive emotions can promote physical and psychological well-being, free resources, aid learning and health behaviour; positive clients elicit more social support.

studies.title: Vaillant (2000): longitudinal study of inner-city boys
studies.finding: Used in Egan's example: a man from a disadvantaged group (mean IQ 80) became a successful businessman, showing resilience a counsellor could tap.

studies.title: Carton, Kessler & Pape (1999)
studies.finding: The ability to read nonverbal messages is a factor in establishing and maintaining relationships.

studies.title: Wahlstein (1991)
studies.finding: It is not easy for clients to fake nonverbal behaviour.

studies.title: Costanzo (1992)
studies.finding: Trainees can learn to identify useful nonverbal messages, clues and modifiers by watching videotaped interactions, including their own.

studies.title: Fauth & Williams (2005): helpers' internal conversations
studies.finding: Helpers' internal conversations were generally helpful rather than hindering, from both trainee and student-client perspectives.

studies.title: Hill, Thompson, Cogar & Denman (1993): covert processes
studies.finding: Clients and therapists are more or less aware of each other's covert processes, but helpers were poor at determining what clients left unsaid.

studies.title: Klein: naturalistic decision making
studies.finding: Fast on-the-spot decisions by experts such as firefighters and pilots make sense when the deciders are skilled and experienced.

studies.finding: People with this style ('it will never go away', 'it affects everything', 'it is my fault') tend to end up with poorer health.

examples.title: SOLER in an Indian college counselling room
examples.text: A student comes in upset about backlogs. The counsellor turns her chair slightly toward him (Squarely, but angled so it is not intimidating), uncrosses her arms (Open), leans forward a little when he starts to describe his father's reaction (Lean), keeps natural eye contact while letting him look down when ashamed (Eye contact), and stops tapping her pen (Relaxed).

examples.title: Tape-recorder listening at home
examples.text: A teenager says 'You're not listening!' and the parent repeats the last sentence word for word while scrolling on the phone. The words were heard, but the teen wanted the parent to be present - that is the difference Egan draws.

examples.title: Full point of view
examples.text: A client says: 'Engineering is a waste for me (view) because I hate coding (reason) - last semester I failed both programming papers (illustration). But I could be wrong; maybe it's just the teaching (openness).' All four parts are there.

examples.title: Evaluative listening among friends
examples.text: A friend shares that she is still hurt by a break-up from a year ago, and you immediately say 'Move on yaar, it's been a year!' That is evaluative listening turning into advice before understanding.

examples.title: Benign interrupting
examples.text: A client talks non-stop for ten minutes about family, job and health. The counsellor raises a hand gently and says, 'You've covered a lot - let me check I've got the main points.' This interruption serves dialogue rather than cutting the client off.

checks.q: According to Egan, how does society generally ensure children develop communication skills?

practice.answer: SOLER is Egan's acronym for the nonverbal skills of visibly tuning in to clients: face the client Squarely, adopt an Open posture, Lean toward the client at times, maintain good Eye contact, and be relatively Relaxed or natural. Egan stresses it is a culture-sensitive framework, not a rigid set of rules, and that it reflects the helper's inner attitudes of respect and empathy.

Clinical drift is the risk, described by Bricker, Glat and Stover, that a helper who has no framework for organising what clients say will let therapy wander away from objective, recognisable goals. Familiarity with a schema of experiences, thoughts, behaviours and emotions instead fosters "clinical mindfulness" and keeps therapy on track.

Honest signals, a term from Pentland, are nonverbal signals that are largely automatic, autonomic and unconscious, which makes them hard to fake. He groups them into activity, interest, mimicry and consistency. They influence the other person, so clients read the kind of helper you are through them - genuineness cannot be faked.

Tough-minded listening means hearing not only clients' stories but the slant or spin they put on them, and detecting gaps, distortions and dissonance in their experienced reality. A client's experience is real and must be understood, but reality cannot be ignored: to be client-centred, the helper must first be reality-centred (e.g., Jennie believing she "got what she deserved").

practice.q: Distinguish between benign and malignant interrupting.
practice.answer: Malignant interrupting is cutting a client off mid-thought because the helper wants to say something important; it stops listening. Benign interrupting gently breaks into a monologue - for example to check that the helper has understood several points - and promotes dialogue serving problem management. Egan notes cultural differences in storytelling must be considered.

practice.q: Explain the four requirements of true dialogue according to Egan.
practice.answer:
Egan argues that communication competence means more than mastering individual skills; it means using them in the service of dialogue. He gives four requirements.

Turn taking: dialogue is interactive - one speaks, then the other. Monologues by either party, whether endless client stories or helper lectures, add no value; monologues isolate while dialogue demands engagement. Turn taking allows mutual learning: helpers base interventions on what they learn, and clients come to understand themselves.

Connecting: each party's remarks should link to what the other has said. Talking past each other produces alternating monologues, which have no place in therapy. Both must actively listen and respond to what they think the other means.

Mutual influencing: both are open to being influenced. This echoes the social-influence dimension of helping; open-minded helpers learn from clients, and clients cannot stay in the driver's seat without influencing helpers. Fowers and Davidov link "openness to the other" with handling diversity.

Cocreating outcomes: good dialogue produces outcomes that benefit both. The counsellor is a catalyst, neither telling clients what to do nor leaving them alone; neither party knows the outcome beforehand. Only clients can change themselves.

Dialogue, shaped by respect and empathy, is the integrating mechanism; exploitative dialogue is a contradiction in terms.

practice.q: Describe the forms of poor listening discussed by Egan.
practice.answer:
Egan stresses that effective listening is an activity requiring work, not a state of mind. Everyone has been both perpetrator and victim of four forms of inadequate listening.

Nonlistening: going through the motions without engagement. Kieran, asked by Jennifer what he would do about the counselling centre's problem, cannot answer because he had tuned her out. Even good helpers can drift when hearing similar stories, forgetting each is unique.

Partial listening: skimming the surface, catching bits but missing essentials. Janice half-listens to Dean's account of a disastrous recruiter meeting; her attempt at understanding rings hollow. Egan considers it potentially worse than nonlistening because it is phony.

Tape-recorder listening: being able to repeat the client's words without being present psychologically, socially and emotionally. A person accused of not listening who protests that they can repeat everything does not comfort the accuser; clients want a live counsellor, not a recorder.

Rehearsing: working out one's reply while the client speaks. Novice Sid dismisses dream interpretation and misses that Casey is disturbed by his dreams. Effective helpers listen to themes and core messages, never need to rehearse, and pause after a client speaks because they have listened and want to respond helpfully.

practice.q: Explain the ways in which nonverbal behaviour modifies verbal messages, with examples.
practice.answer:
Egan explains that besides being a channel in its own right, clients' nonverbal behaviour - facial expressions, bodily motions and voice quality - modifies and punctuates speech, much as punctuation and underlining do in writing. Because it is spontaneous it "leaks" real meaning, and clients find it hard to fake (Wahlstein). He describes five ways, illustrated with Jennie and Denise.

1. Confirming or repeating: when Denise's response hits the mark, Jennie says "That's right!", her eyes light up, she leans forward and her voice is animated.
2. Denying or confusing: challenged, Jennie denies being upset but her voice falters and her upper lip quivers; the nonverbal carries the real message.
3. Strengthening or emphasising: asked to question her boss about "erratic behaviour," Jennie says in a startled voice she could not, slouching and putting her face in her hands.
4. Adding intensity: Jennie says she dislikes being confronted before being understood, then stares fixedly and silently with a frown.
5. Controlling or regulating: in a group, Tom looks away when Nina is about to speak to him, and she stays silent.

Egan cautions that helpers should "read" rather than interpret, understand rather than dissect, and rely on context; novices who seize on a half-smile or frown can lose the person.

practice.q: Explain filtered, evaluative and stereotype-based listening as forms of distorted listening.
practice.answer:
Egan calls distorted listening the shadow side because helpers never intend it, yet slip into it unaware, and it blocks open-minded listening.

Filtered listening: completely unbiased listening is impossible. Socialisation gives us personal, familial, sociological and cultural filters; Hall noted culture is a selective screen deciding what we notice and ignore. Filters give structure but introduce unnoticed bias, and the stronger the cultural filters, the greater the bias - e.g., a white, middle-class helper listening to a poor farmer or an urban African American mother. Helpers may pigeonhole by gender, race, religion and so on, so self-knowledge that roots out prejudice is essential.

Evaluative listening: judging what one hears as good/bad, right/wrong while listening. Jennie's friend tells her to forget the rape and get on with life - evaluation becoming advice. Clients should first be understood, then challenged if needed. Productive evaluation exists, and judgment cannot be fully suspended, but it can be set aside for the time being to understand clients from the inside.

Stereotype-based listening: labels replace people, as when a doctor called Egan "the hernia in 304." Diagnostic labels are interpretations, not understandings; one can be "correct" and still lose the person. The client should remain "figure" and theories "ground."

practice.q: Discuss visibly tuning in and the SOLER guidelines. How should a helper use them in a culturally sensitive way?
practice.answer:
Introduction

Egan begins Part II of The Skilled Helper with empathic presence because simply being with someone can matter deeply - sitting with a friend in hospital or with a newly widowed man comforts them even when little is said. Helping demands a robust, intense presence; Geller and Greenberg describe therapeutic presence as a foundational stance that supports deep listening. Visibly tuning in expresses empathy, tells clients the helper is with them, and positions the helper to listen. It is shown both physically and psychologically.

Nonverbal behaviour as the medium

Visibly tuning in works largely through nonverbal behaviour. Highlen and Hill note that nonverbal behaviours regulate conversation, communicate emotion, modify verbal messages, signal the state of the relationship, reveal self-perceptions and leak what is unspoken. Egan lists eight channels: bodily behaviour, eye behaviour, facial expressions, voice-related behaviour, autonomic responses, physical characteristics, space and general appearance. Clients read the quality of the helper's presence in these cues: attentive presence invites trust and exploration, half-hearted presence breeds distrust. Clients can also misread the helper - a comfortable distance may feel too close, a thoughtful silence may embarrass.

The SOLER guidelines

S - face the client Squarely: adopt a posture of involvement that says "I'm here with you." Not to be taken literally; if facing squarely feels threatening, an angle is fine. The point is quality of presence, not inches and angles.

O - adopt an Open posture: crossed arms and legs may signal lessened availability; openness is seen as nondefensive. Crossed legs do not prove disengagement, but the helper should ask how far posture communicates openness.

L - Lean toward the client at times: like engaged diners leaning over a table, a slight forward lean shows interest, while slouching may signal boredom. Leaning too far or too soon may frighten a client. Metaphorically, lean means bodily and mental flexibility.

E - maintain good Eye contact: fairly steady but not staring; occasionally looking away is natural, but frequent looking away may reveal reluctance or discomfort.

R - be Relaxed or natural: no fidgeting or distracting expressions, and comfort in using the body as a vehicle of contact, which puts clients at ease.

Cultural sensitivity and adaptation

Egan repeatedly ties each guideline to North American culture and calls SOLER only a framework. Eye contact is the clearest example: in some cultures much eye contact, especially with authority figures, is inappropriate, as Egan learned from Asian students and clients. Givens' nonverbal dictionary underlines that assuming gestures mean the same everywhere is wrong and sometimes dangerous. The SOLAR adaptation shows flexible use: a counsellor teaching visually impaired students found eye contact irrelevant but voice direction crucial, and replaced E with "Aim" - pointing head and body at the client so they hear attention.

Using SOLER genuinely

Egan insists the skills are phony unless driven by respect and empathy; his doctor said reassuring words while his rushed manner said otherwise. Helpers should be mindful but not preoccupied with their bodies, read their own reactions (tense muscles signalling anxiety), restrain impulsive signals out of respect, and "punctuate" constructive client statements, as Denise does by leaning forward and nodding. Pentland's honest signals show that genuineness cannot be faked. Box 3.1 offers self-check questions on attitudes, presence and distractions.

Conclusion

Visibly tuning in is the doorway to listening. SOLER gives a memorable framework, but its value lies in conveying an inner attitude of respectful involvement in a form the particular client - shaped by culture and circumstance - can recognise. Applied rigidly, it becomes technique; applied flexibly, it lets clients see the helper's care.

practice.q: Explain what clients talk about when they tell their stories, according to Egan's framework of focused listening. Illustrate with the case of Jennie.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Egan describes helping as a "talking game" in which the quality of talk is crucial. Listening at its best is both focused and unbiased. He offers two aids to focus: the problem-management model, which is not tied to any school and helps organise what is heard without prejudice, and a view of personality. Pervin defines personality as the organisation of cognitions, affects and behaviours giving coherence to a person's life, and Rasmussen adds the "activating event." Clients thus tell stories in terms of experiences, thoughts, behaviours and feelings, and helpers are listening to personalities at work. Bricker, Glat and Stover argue such a framework fosters clinical mindfulness and prevents clinical drift.

Experiences

Experiences are what happens to clients. Jennie spoke of being raped, belittled and ignored. Listening to experiences is vital, but such stories are often incomplete and tinged with victimhood, blaming others or the world. Some internal experiences feel out of control ("I just can't stop thinking of him"). Some clients are genuinely victimised and need social change - one counsellor's client needed the courts to keep a brutal husband away - while others use experiences to avoid responsibility. Recalling Sykes' "nation of victims," Egan asks helpers to distinguish whiners from victims and to respect negative experiences while helping clients move beyond them.

Thoughts

Clients share thinking through points of view, intentions, decisions and proposals. A full point of view includes the view, reasons, an illustration and openness to change. Jennie's view that "the system" cannot be trusted strongly shapes her behaviour; Denise understands its origins but knows its consequences need exploring, since points of view can be self-enhancing or self-limiting. Proposals, like Lydia's case for quitting her job, include what, why and implications. A fully shared decision includes the decision, reasons, implications for self and others and openness to review. Jennie's languid announcement that she will avoid jobs involving race or gender battles carries an implied "don't argue," but its tone suggests it may not be final.

Behaviours

Clients describe what they do or fail to do, externally (drinking) or internally (daydreaming). Jennie pulled away from family and friends. Many clients avoid discussing behaviour because it raises personal responsibility.

Feelings, emotions and moods

Affect runs through everything like a river. Feelings pervade life, affect its quality and drive behaviour (Lang's "action dispositions"). Jennie spoke of shame, betrayal and anger. Mayer and Salovey's four branches of emotional intelligence help helpers perceive and manage emotion. Clients often express feelings nonverbally, as when Jennie says she does not mind talking about herself while looking away and frowning.

Strengths, nonverbal messages and the integrated narrative

Egan adds listening for strengths - poor counsellors listen only for problems - and for nonverbal modifiers. Clients mix all these elements into an integrated narrative. Jennie later reauthors her story: after meeting a woman with a similar history, she decides to broaden her social life and rethink her work, showing experiences, views, decisions and proposals woven together.

Conclusion

Egan's framework turns a stream of talk into an organised picture without forcing it into a theory. With Jennie, it lets Denise see how her experiences, distrustful thinking, withdrawal and depression connect, and where change might start. But Egan warns against being a "vacuum cleaner": the purpose is meaning that helps clients move forward.

practice.q: Discuss 'processing what you hear' and 'listening to oneself' as described by Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Egan notes that as we listen we inevitably process what we hear; the task is to be a thoughtful processor rather than a careless one. He offers four guidelines for thoughtful processing and then turns to the helper's own internal conversation.

1. Understand clients through context

Clients are more than the sum of their messages. Deep listening hears clients as shaped by the contexts in which they live (Cook). Tiedens and Leach argue emotions cannot be understood apart from social relationships and groups. Culture, personality, ethnicity, education, economic status and other diversity factors form the context of problems, whether mentioned or not. Denise hears Jennie through her history: a conservative Catholic upbringing in which the church was a refuge, a first venture into a white, secular college, the discovery she was academically average, withdrawal from family, church and friends after the rape and investigation, and current underemployment. Denise sees the rape as a social event and considers how Jennie may feel about her as a helper, yet she does not let context define Jennie or get lost in it.

2. Identify key messages and feelings

Helpers must avoid information overload by identifying what is key to the purpose of helping, not to a theory. As Jennie describes her intention to pursue her case collapsing into anger and numbness, Denise asks herself: what are the main points, themes, decisions and proposals; what does Jennie want understood; how is the dialogue going? Duncan's feedback surveys support this by opening two-way feedback.

3. Hear the slant or spin

Tough-minded listening detects gaps, distortions and dissonance. A client's self-perception as ugly is real, but so are the facts. Jennie's claim that she got what she deserved for aiming too high is her spin; understanding it differs from accepting it. Egan's principle: to be client-centred, be reality-centred first.

4. Muse on what's missing

Clients omit feelings, reasons, implications, resources or flexibility. Jennie mentions a call from an old friend without saying how she felt, and refuses her brother's job offer without reasons before changing the subject. This is not a hunt for hidden material; knowing what full stories look like, Denise notices gaps and uses clinical judgment (largely common sense) about asking. Her question reveals Jennie has ruled out family involvement.

Listening to oneself

The internal conversation is what helpers say to themselves during sessions. Listening on a "second channel" - to one's thoughts, nonverbal behaviour and emotions - is a positive self-consciousness that reveals what might help and what blocks presence. Egan's own example: with an excited friend fresh from psychiatric hospitalisations, he kept finding his arms and legs crossed, revealing concern for his own security. Second-channel messages may concern the helper ("my mind is wandering"), the client ("her self-pity blocks action; go slow") or the relationship ("time to test the waters"). Fauth and Williams found such internal conversations generally helpful rather than hindering. Clients have internal conversations too; Hill and colleagues found helpers knew clients left things unsaid but could not tell what. Moving key points from the client's internal conversation into dialogue is a later task.

Conclusion

Processing and self-listening turn raw listening into understanding. Context, key messages, spin and gaps make sense of the client; the second channel keeps the helper honest about what they bring. Together they guard against the distortions Egan describes in the shadow side.

practice.q: 'The shadow side of listening' - critically discuss the forms of distorted listening described by Egan and their implications for counsellors.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Egan argues that listening is harder than it sounds. Distortions pervade everyday communication and creep into helping, sometimes several at once. He calls them the shadow side because helpers never intend them and often fail to notice them, yet they block the open-minded listening needed for dialogue. He lists six forms.

1. Filtered listening

Nobody listens without bias. Socialisation gives personal, familial, sociological and cultural filters; Hall saw culture as a selective screen deciding what we notice. Filters give structure but bias listening invisibly, and the stronger the cultural filters, the greater the bias. A white, middle-class helper may distort the stories of a wealthy Asian client, an African American mother from a ghetto, or a poor farmer. Helpers may pigeonhole by gender, race, sexual orientation, religion or lifestyle. The remedy is self-knowledge that roots out prejudice.

2. Evaluative listening

Most people judge as they listen - good/bad, right/wrong, relevant/irrelevant. Jennie's friend, hearing that the rape still haunts her, tells her to forget it and get on with life; evaluation becomes advice and puts clients off. Egan's rule: understand first, then challenge if needed. He concedes that productive evaluation exists and judgment cannot be wholly suspended, but it can be set aside for now to understand clients from the inside.

3. Stereotype-based listening

Being called "the hernia in 304" shows how labels depersonalise. Training labels (paranoid, borderline) and personality types can block empathy; diagnosis can take precedence over the person. Labels are interpretations, not understanding - one can be correct and still lose the person. Gestalt terms help: client as figure, theory as ground.

4. Fact-centred rather than person-centred listening

Some helpers fire informational questions as if facts cure. The antidote is contextual listening for themes. Denise notices Jennie's pessimistic explanatory style (Peterson, Seligman & Vaillant) - "it will never go away," "it is my fault" - and, since research links it to poorer health, hypothesises a link with her headaches and gastric problems.

5. Sympathetic listening

Clients' misery invites sympathy strong enough to distort. Liz, recently widowed, wanted to hold Ben, who lost his wife and daughter to a tornado; she heard his loss but only half heard his implication that it excused him from moving on. Sympathy makes the helper an accomplice who takes sides without the full story and can reinforce self-pity, which drives out action.

6. Interrupting

Egan includes it reluctantly. Interrupting stops listening and often reflects rehearsing, but because helping is a dialogue he distinguishes malignant interrupting (cutting off mid-thought) from benign interrupting (gently breaking a monologue to check understanding), mindful of cultural storytelling styles.

Critical evaluation and implications

Egan's list is practical rather than exhaustive - he describes "some forms," and related problems such as rehearsing appear earlier under poor listening. His nuance is a strength: evaluation and interrupting each have productive versions, and sympathy has a place in life, so the issue is distortion, not the behaviours themselves. He identifies a root cause: the unexamined belief that open-minded listening equals approval, when in fact it simply enables understanding. The stakes are high: like a slightly crooked foundation that makes a ninth floor look like the Leaning Tower of Pisa, small early errors grow.

Conclusion

The shadow side reminds counsellors that listening is a discipline. Self-knowledge, suspending judgment, keeping the person as figure, listening for themes, using empathy rather than sympathy, and interrupting only to serve dialogue protect the foundation skill on which all helping rests.

practice.q: Discuss how listening relates to the key ingredients of successful therapy, using Egan's cases.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Egan closes the chapter by applying listening to the key ingredients of successful therapy outlined in Chapter 1. He uses two cases: Denise working with Jennie, and Laura working with Karl, a veteran with PTSD who also gains support from Peter, his "buddy." Eight targets of listening emerge.

1. Listening to the client

Helpers attend to what clients see as important: their stories, expectations, resources, degree of collaboration, struggles with obstacles, reactions to the helper, willingness to be in the driver's seat, desired outcomes, engagement with the treatment method, emotions, hesitations and contextual factors. Denise listens for signs of hope, especially Jennie's "tiny steps" back into community. Laura notices Karl's emphasis on how helpful Peter is, even hinting he gets more from Peter than from sessions, and treats this as material for feedback.

2. Listening to ourselves as therapists

Helpers monitor their impact, uncertainties, how the client affects them, mistakes, emotions, genuineness and the effectiveness of their method, without self-preoccupation. Laura accepts that Peter may be producing more results because client outcomes are the bottom line; the relationship is not an end in itself. Denise senses she should encourage Jennie further into the driver's seat.

3. Listening to the relationship

This includes what is working, the quality of collaboration and dialogue, mutual influence and ruptures. Karl treats Laura as an authority figure to be managed and always says they are doing "just fine," keeping her at arm's length. As he is progressing, Laura does not push: good outcomes trump ideal relationships.

4. Listening to the flow of communication and dialogue

Helpers tailor their communication to clients' responses and abilities. Denise sees Jennie's communication skills as a resource for re-entering community; Karl treats conversation as a power game, but Laura has no need to be one up, so she leaves well enough alone.

5. Listening to two-way feedback

Helpers attend to formal and informal feedback on progress and session quality. Denise uses Duncan's surveys; Laura hears Karl's defensiveness, wonders what she might be doing to cause it, and learns of his substantial progress by debriefing his sessions with Peter.

6. Listening to the flow of the method of treatment

Helpers check that clients understand and can collaborate on the method - here the problem-management process - and watch for commitment. Both clients manage it, Jennie more proactively.

7. Listening to the decisions being made

Helpers note clients' decision style (Kahneman's fast or slow) and awareness of consequences. Jennie is thoughtful but does not always review consequences; Karl is abrupt, as in rejecting feedback surveys. Helpers watch their own decisions too: Denise worries she influences too much, Laura whether she should be more forceful. Klein's research shows fast expert decisions work when the expert is skilled and experienced; helpers must also be principled, and accept the uncertainty at the heart of decisions.

8. Listening to assumptions, beliefs, values, norms, ethical and moral issues

This package, including culture, runs through stories. Jennie's religious sensitivities are a subtext and a resource for recovery. Karl's fundamentalist upbringing left "musts," loyalty transferred to his platoon, and a sense of betrayal at surviving when buddies died.

Conclusion

This section broadens listening from the client's words to the whole therapeutic system - client, helper, relationship, dialogue, feedback, method, decisions and values - all judged by outcomes.

summary: Research neglects the communication skills needed for the helping relationship; Egan treats them as a key ingredient, built on everyday interpersonal skills (p. 72).
True dialogue needs turn taking, connecting, mutual influencing and cocreating outcomes; dialogue is the integrating mechanism of communication competence (pp. 73-74).
Empathic presence - visibly tuning in - tells clients the helper is with them; Geller and Greenberg call therapeutic presence foundational (p. 74).
Nonverbal behaviour (eight channels) regulates conversation, conveys emotion and modifies words; helpers must monitor their own signals without preoccupation (pp. 75-77).
SOLER - Squarely, Open, Lean, Eye contact, Relaxed - is a culture-sensitive framework, adaptable as SOLAR ('Aim') for visually impaired clients (pp. 77-78).
Pentland's honest signals show genuineness cannot be faked; Richmond and McCroskey list six myths about nonverbal behaviour (p. 79).
Full listening is active, accurate and for meaning; poor listening includes nonlistening, partial, tape-recorder listening and rehearsing (pp. 80-82).
Empathic listening, Rogers' 'unappreciated way of being', leads to empathic understanding and responding (p. 82).
Focused listening organises clients' stories into experiences, thoughts, behaviours and affect, preventing clinical drift (pp. 83-84).
Experience stories often carry victimhood; helpers distinguish real victims from whiners and help clients move beyond experiences (p. 85).
Thoughts are shared as points of view, intentions, proposals and decisions, each with a 'full' form (pp. 85-87).
Emotions pervade life, affect its quality and drive behaviour; emotional intelligence and positive emotions are resources (pp. 88-89).
Successful counsellors listen for strengths and resources, not just problems (pp. 89-90).
Clients' nonverbal behaviour leaks meaning and modifies speech in five ways; context is key and overinterpretation loses the person (pp. 90-91).
Narrative therapy helps clients integrate their story and reauthor it, as Jennie does (pp. 91-93).
Thoughtful processing: understand through context, identify key messages, hear the spin, muse on what's missing (pp. 93-96).
Helpers listen to their internal conversation on a 'second channel'; research finds it mostly helpful (pp. 96-97).
Listening extends to the key ingredients of therapy: client, self, relationship, dialogue, feedback, method, decisions and values (pp. 97-100).
Shadow-side distorted listening: filtered, evaluative, stereotype-based, fact-centred, sympathetic, and (with reservations) interrupting (pp. 100-103).
Small early listening errors snowball; tuning in and open-minded listening are foundation skills (p. 103).
